Thompson's and John Van Seters's mid-1970s arguments (Thompson's The Historicity of the Patriarchal Narratives, De Gruyter, 1974; Van Seters's Abraham in History and Tradition, 1975) that the patriarchal narratives are literary constructions reflecting a much later period than they claim to depict, and Kenneth Kitchen's traditionalist rebuttal (On the Reliability of the Old Testament, Eerdmans, 2003). No contemporary extra-biblical text names Abraham or anyone matching his specific narrative; the debate is over what, if anything, the internal evidence of Genesis's own composition can establish about a period centuries before any surviving manuscript.

Matthew's use of the name is not making a historicity claim so much as invoking a genealogical and covenantal starting point his Jewish audience would recognize instantly — the same rhetorical move the genealogy's whole three-part structure (1:17) is built around.

Cited in: Matthew 1:1-2, 1:17; see Note 1.

ALLEGORICAL VS. SINGLE-POINT PARABLE INTERPRETATION (JULICHER/JEREMIAS DEBATE)

The long-running, still-unresolved source-critical debate over whether Jesus's parables were originally simple, one-point illustrative comparisons — with detailed, multi-referent allegorical readings like the sower's point-by-point explanation (13:18-23) added later by the church — or whether at least some allegorical framing goes back to Jesus's own original telling. Adolf Jülicher's 1888-1899 study established the single-point position [219]; Joachim Jeremias's form-critical work reached a related but distinct conclusion, treating the sower's explanation specifically as a later missionary-situation overlay [220]; more recent scholarship, including Klyne Snodgrass and Craig Blomberg, argues the single-point rule overcorrected and that multi-referent readings need not be later inventions [221]. No side of this debate has settled the question.

ANDREW

Brother of Simon Peter (see SIMON PETER) and, with him, one of the first two fishermen called (Matthew 4:18-20). Unlike nearly every other name among the Twelve, "Andrew" is a Greek name (*Andreas*, "manly") rather than a Hebrew or Aramaic one — not unheard of for a 1st-century Galilean Jew given the region's Greek-influenced culture, but a small, real detail distinguishing him from his brother's Semitic name.

Beyond the call narratives and apostle lists, nothing about Andrew survives from any 1st-century source, Christian or otherwise. His much-repeated later biography — a missionary career culminating in crucifixion on an X-shaped ("saltire") cross — is a medieval invention with no source earlier than roughly the 10th century; the saltire cross is not attested at all in antiquity as his manner of death. His earliest substantial biographical text is the apocryphal *Acts of Andrew* (2nd-3rd century), a genre of writing composed to give later Christian communities an apostolic founder, not a contemporary eyewitness record.

Cited in: Matthew 4:18; see SIMON PETER.

ANGAREIA (ROMAN IMPRESSMENT PRACTICE)

The attested Roman legal practice, named by a Greek verb (angareuo) borrowed from a Persian term for state courier-relay service, of compelling a civilian to carry a soldier's pack or equipment for a fixed distance — one Roman mile — without payment or consent. Named directly in Matthew 5:41's "if anyone forces you to go one mile," independently attested in the same period by the Stoic philosopher Epictetus, and used again by Matthew himself for Simon of Cyrene's forced carrying of Jesus's cross (27:32) [118] [119] [120].

ARCHELAUS

Herod the Great's son by his Samaritan wife Malthace, and the ruler Matthew's nativity account has Joseph fear when considering a return to Judea from Egypt (2:22): "when he heard that Archelaus did reign in Judaea in the room of his father Herod, he was afraid to go thither" — the reason the family settles in Nazareth instead. Herod's will split his kingdom three ways among sons; Archelaus received the largest share (Judea, Samaria, and Idumea) but only the lesser title of ethnarch, pending Rome's confirmation — a step down from the "king" title his father had used.

Josephus (Jewish Antiquities 17.213–218, 17.339–18.2; Jewish War 2.111–113) is the entire independent record of his rule, and it is short and unflattering: he opened his reign having Roman troops suppress a Passover riot in the Temple, with several thousand reportedly killed, and governed harshly enough afterward that in his tenth year (6 CE) a joint delegation of his own Jewish and Samaritan subjects traveled to Rome to formally accuse him before Augustus. Augustus deposed him, confiscated his territory, and exiled him to Vienne, a city in Roman Gaul, where no surviving source records anything further about him. Judea, Samaria, and Idumea were then folded into a Roman province under prefects appointed directly from Rome — Pontius Pilate, decades later, held that same office Archelaus's deposition created (see PONTIUS PILATE).

Cited in: Matthew 2:22.

ARIMATHEA

The hometown given for Joseph, the wealthy follower who requests Jesus's body and provides the tomb for burial (Matthew 27:57-60). Unlike most places named in Matthew's Passion narrative, Arimathea's location is genuinely, honestly unresolved — not a live scholarly dispute between two identifiable candidates, but a case where the town itself cannot be confidently placed on a map at all.

The standard proposal, traceable to the 4th-century church historian Eusebius of Caesarea in his Onomasticon (a gazetteer of biblical place-names), identifies Arimathea with the Old Testament town of Ramathaim-Zophim — the birthplace of the prophet Samuel (1 Samuel 1:1) — and locates it near Diospolis (modern Lod), commonly associated today with the Palestinian village of Rentis (also transliterated Rantis), in the hill country of Ephraim northwest of Jerusalem. But Eusebius was writing some three centuries after the events he was describing, and by his own era, independent memory of the original site's exact location had already faded; his identification is a reasonable inference built on similar-sounding names and regional tradition, not a preserved contemporary record. Other candidate identifications for Ramathaim-Zophim itself remain in play in Old Testament scholarship independent of the New Testament question, including the village of Nabi Samwil closer to Jerusalem — meaning the uncertainty compounds rather than resolves the further back it is traced.

Honest treatment of this one is simple: no one currently knows, with confidence, exactly where Arimathea was.

Cited in: Matthew 27:57.

BAPTISM (FIRST-CENTURY JEWISH IMMERSION PRACTICE)

Ritual water immersion, the practice John is best known for and the rite Jesus undergoes at the end of this chapter (3:13-17). First-century Judaism already practiced various forms of ritual washing for purity, and the initiatory washings at Qumran are the closest attested regional parallel to John's version of the practice [92], though John's baptism is generally read by scholars as distinctive in being a one-time, public rite of repentance rather than the Qumran community's repeated purificatory washing. Josephus's independent account frames the purpose slightly differently than the Synoptic Gospels do — purification of the body for people already made righteous, rather than the Synoptics' baptism `for the forgiveness of sins'' — a real, if subtle, divergence in how the same basic practice was understood by two separate ancient sources.

BARABBAS

The prisoner Matthew 27:16–26 (paralleled in Mark 15:6–15, Luke 23:18–25, John 18:39–40) has Pilate offer the Jerusalem crowd as an alternative release to Jesus, under a stated Passover-pardon custom that has zero attestation in any Roman or Jewish source outside the Gospels themselves. The crowd chooses Barabbas — described in Matthew as "a notable prisoner" and in Mark and Luke as a man jailed for insurrection and murder — and Jesus is crucified instead.

The name itself carries a second layer of significance. "Bar-abbas" is Aramaic for "son of the father," and a number of ancient manuscripts of Matthew — most notably reflected in a Syriac tradition possibly reaching back to the 5th century, and in a Greek scholion (marginal note) attributed in some manuscripts to Origen (early 3rd century CE) — give his full name as "Jesus Barabbas," making the choice put to the crowd "Jesus Barabbas, son of the father" against "Jesus who is called Christ": two men sharing the same given name, one carrying a patronymic that echoes Jesus's own claimed relationship to God. Origen, in the surviving note attributed to him, says he found "Barabbas called Jesus" in "very old copies" but argued against the reading, on grounds later scholars generally read as theological discomfort at "Jesus" being shared with a convicted insurrectionist — meaning the shorter, name-less "Barabbas" that became the standard text may itself be the edited version, not the original one. No surviving Greek manuscript containing the longer reading predates the 10th century, though the scholion's attribution to Origen, if genuine, would push awareness of the variant back roughly seven centuries earlier than the manuscripts themselves.

Cited in: Matthew 27:16–26.

BARTHOLOMEW

Named in all four apostle lists (Matthew 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:14; Acts 1:13), always paired with Philip, but never once given an action, saying, or story of his own anywhere in the New Testament. "Bartholomew" is not, strictly, a personal name — it is Aramaic *bar-Tolmai*, "son of Tolmai" (or Talmai), a patronymic rather than a given name, comparable to "Johnson" originally meaning "son of John." This has long led scholars to suspect Bartholomew had another, personal name the Gospels simply don't record alongside his patronymic.

The leading candidate is Nathanael, who appears only in John's Gospel (John 1:45-51, 21:2) and is introduced by Philip in nearly the same narrative position the Synoptics give Bartholomew — but John never calls Nathanael one of the Twelve, and none of the Synoptic apostle lists ever use the name Nathanael. The identification is old, widespread, and plausible, but it is an inference built from narrative position and pairing with Philip, not something any text states outright — on the same unresolved footing as the Matthew/Levi and Thaddaeus/Judas-son-of-James identifications elsewhere in this list.

As with most of the Twelve, everything claimed about Bartholomew beyond the bare name — a missionary field in Armenia or India, a martyrdom by flaying — comes from apocryphal Acts composed centuries later, not any contemporary record.

Cited in: Matthew 10:3.

BATHSHEBA

Named nowhere in Matthew's genealogy — Matthew 1:6 calls her only "the wife of Uriah," the sole one of the genealogy's four women identified through a man's name rather than her own (see RUTH for the naming pattern Matthew otherwise follows). Her story is told across 2 Samuel 11-12. While her husband Uriah is at the front with the rest of David's army, David — who has stayed behind in Jerusalem — sees her bathing, sends for her, and sleeps with her (11:1-4); she becomes pregnant (11:5). David recalls Uriah from the field hoping he will sleep with his own wife and obscure the timing, but Uriah refuses, unwilling to enjoy his home while his fellow soldiers remain in the field (11:6-13). David then has Uriah placed at the front of the fiercest fighting with support withdrawn, engineering his death in battle (11:14-17), after which David marries Bathsheba. The prophet Nathan confronts David over the affair (12:1-14); the child of the union dies, narrated as direct consequence (12:15-19); a second son, Solomon, is born of the same marriage afterward (12:24-25) and eventually succeeds David as king.

Uriah is identified throughout as "the Hittite" (2 Samuel 11:3 and repeatedly thereafter) and appears by name among the elite corps of warriors scripture calls "the Thirty" (2 Samuel 23:24-39 lists the group, ending with Uriah; the roster's own count, as verse 39 states, actually runs to thirty-seven) — a non-Israelite serving among David's own most trusted soldiers. Scripture never states that Bathsheba herself was of foreign origin, only her husband; but set beside Tamar, Rahab, and Ruth the Moabite (see MOAB, RUTH), Uriah's ethnicity reads as at minimum a quiet fourth echo of the same foreign-origin thread running through the other three names in Matthew's list, even though this time the label attaches to the husband rather than the wife.

Richard Bauckham's Gospel Women: Studies of the Named Women in the Gospels (Eerdmans, 2002) reads Matthew's choice of "the wife of Uriah" over "Bathsheba" as deliberate rather than incidental: it keeps Uriah — the wronged, murdered party — inside the sentence, and with him the plain fact that David's line continues through an act of adultery and an engineered killing, not merely an unnamed irregularity. Matthew had Mary's own unmarried pregnancy to introduce two verses later (1:18-25); the genealogy's run of scandal-adjacent women, ending on this one, has been read as priming the reader not to flinch from Mary's circumstance either.

Cited in: Matthew 1:6; see RUTH.

BEATITUDE (ASHREI FORM)

The Hebrew Bible's own wisdom-literature ashrei ("happy is," "blessed is") blessing formula, exemplified by Psalm 1:1 and Psalm 32:1, and the recognized literary genre Matthew's eight (or nine) Beatitudes work within rather than invent (5:3-12). The form's first eight instances share a uniform third-person construction; the final, on persecution, shifts to direct second-person address, a grammatical seam commentators read as marking Matthew's own redactional expansion of an inherited core [109] [110].

BETHANY

A village on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, roughly two and a half kilometers (a mile and a half) from Jerusalem on the road to Jericho — the home, in John's Gospel, of Lazarus, Martha, and Mary, and, in Matthew, the site of Simon the Leper's house where a woman anoints Jesus shortly before the Passion (26:6-13), as well as Jesus's evident base of operations during Passion week (21:17). The ancient village's name survives directly in its modern successor, al-Eizariya — Arabic for "place of Lazarus" — a Palestinian town that has grown over and absorbed the original site. Franciscan excavations directed by Fr. Sylvester J. Saller between 1949 and 1953 uncovered four superimposed churches next to the traditionally venerated Tomb of Lazarus, the earliest dating to the 4th or 5th century, along with rock-cut tombs, houses, and pottery attesting occupation back through the Persian and Hellenistic periods — solid, independent confirmation of a long-inhabited site in the right location, even though nothing excavated can specifically confirm the Gospel events said to have happened there.

This Bethany must be kept distinct from "Bethany beyond the Jordan" (John 1:28), a different, second place with the same name, on the opposite side of the country entirely — the location where John the Baptist is said to have been baptizing. Some ancient manuscripts read "Bethabara" there instead, a variant traceable to the 3rd-century scholar Origen, who found no Jordan-side "Bethany" he recognized and proposed the alternate name; modern textual criticism regards "Bethany beyond the Jordan" as the better-attested original reading. The two places sharing a name across two separate Gospel contexts has caused real confusion historically, which is precisely why John's own text bothers to specify "beyond the Jordan" — an ancient author's own disambiguation, doing the same job this entry does now.

Cited in: Matthew 21:17; 26:6.

BETHLEHEM (OF JUDEA)

A small hill-country town in the tribal territory of Judah, roughly eight kilometers south of Jerusalem. Matthew 2:1 calls it "Bethlehem of Judea" specifically to distinguish it from a second, much smaller Bethlehem in Galilee, near Nazareth. As a real, locatable 1st-century village on known Roman-period geography, its existence is not in dispute.

Whether it was actually Jesus's birthplace is a live scholarly question. Matthew (2:1-6) and Luke (2:4-7) both narrate a Bethlehem birth, and Matthew explicitly frames it as fulfilling Micah 5:2's prophecy of a ruler coming out of Bethlehem Ephrathah — but every other independent reference to Jesus anywhere else in the New Testament, without exception, calls him "Jesus of Nazareth," with no indication a Bethlehem birth was widely known or considered relevant. Mainstream critical scholarship (E. P. Sanders, The Historical Figure of Jesus, Penguin Books, 1993) reads this pattern — a prophecy that requires Bethlehem, an infancy account supplying it, and total silence everywhere else in the text — as more consistent with theological placement than preserved memory.

Actual 1st-century Bethlehem was an unremarkable small village, not the grandeur later Christian tradition (the Church of the Nativity, built under Constantine in the 4th century) eventually attached to it; Matthew's own massacre account (2:16) implicitly concedes this scale, describing infant boys killed "two years old and under" within Bethlehem and its immediate vicinity only. Archaeologist Aviram Oshri, who spent roughly a decade excavating the separate, smaller "Bethlehem of Galilee" near Nazareth, argued in a widely discussed article that this site — a seven-kilometer trip from Nazareth, versus the roughly 175-kilometer trip the Judean identification implies — is the geographically more practical birthplace candidate (Oshri, A. (2005). Where was Jesus born? Archaeology, 58(6). Archaeological Institute of America). This is a minority position, not the mainstream reading, but it rests on an actual excavated site rather than argument from silence alone.

Cited in: Matthew 2:1

BETHPHAGE

A small village on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, close to Bethany, on the road that descends toward Jericho — the place where, in all three Synoptic accounts, Jesus sends two disciples ahead to procure the donkey (and, in Matthew's telling, a donkey and a colt together, 21:2-7) for the entry into Jerusalem. The name is generally read as Aramaic for "house of unripe figs."

Bethphage's precise footprint has not been established archaeologically with the confidence available for larger sites — the area has been continuously inhabited, built over, and re-commemorated since antiquity, which has erased or buried whatever first-century structures existed there. Proposals for its exact spot vary: some identify it with the summit area where the Palestinian village of et-Tur now stands, while a Franciscan sanctuary lower on the slope, near the traditional site of Bethany, has marked a different traditional spot since the medieval period. What is not seriously contested, across this range of proposals, is the general location — a village on the Mount of Olives's eastern face, on the Jerusalem-Jericho road, near Bethany — which is exactly the geography the Gospel narrative requires and does not depend on resolving the exact footprint question to be considered a real, located place.

Cited in: Matthew 21:1.

BETHSAIDA

Named alongside Chorazin in Jesus's "woe" saying (Matthew 11:21) and elsewhere in the Gospels as the hometown of Peter, Andrew, and Philip (John 1:44). Unlike Capernaum or Chorazin, Bethsaida's exact location is a live, unresolved archaeological argument rather than a settled identification.

Two sites compete. Et-Tell, an inland mound roughly a mile and a quarter from the current shoreline, has been excavated since 1987 by Rami Arav's Bethsaida Excavations Project, published across the multivolume series Bethsaida: A City by the North Shore of the Sea of Galilee (Arav & Freund, Eds., Truman State University Press, vols. 1–4, 1995–2009); Arav's team argues Iron Age gate remains and a Roman-period building support the identification, and that Jordan delta silting has since pushed the shoreline away from what was a lakeside site in antiquity. El-Araj, which sits directly on the modern shore, has been excavated since 2016 by Mordechai Aviam and R. Steven Notley, whose team has uncovered Roman-period bathhouse remains, a silver coin of Nero (65/66 CE), and a Byzantine-era church tentatively linked to a "Church of the Apostles" described in an 8th-century pilgrim account.

The dispute is documented directly in the scholarly record: Notley, R. S. (2007), "Et-Tell Is Not Bethsaida," Near Eastern Archaeology, 70(4), 220–230, argues against Arav's site on hydrological and shoreline-geology grounds; Arav, R. (2011), "Bethsaida — A Response to Steven Notley," Near Eastern Archaeology, 74, 92–100, rebuts it directly. As of the most recent el-Araj seasons, Arav has called conclusions favoring his rival site "extremely premature" — this is genuinely unresolved between two working excavation teams, not a controversy that has already been settled in the literature.

Cited in: Matthew (beat covering 11:21); see CHORAZIN.

BINDING AND LOOSING (RABBINIC LEGAL AUTHORITY)

The pair of verbs in Jesus's grant to Peter, "whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven" (Matthew 16:19) — standard, technical legal language in Second Temple and early rabbinic Judaism for the authority to rule something forbidden or permitted, as this chapter's own beat on the passage traces in detail through Josephus's description of Pharisaic authority under Salome Alexandra and the Mishnah's routine "forbid/permit" formula [61]. Handing Peter this specific pair of verbs casts him, on the text's own account, in a role a first-century audience would have recognized immediately: the authority to issue binding rulings for the community, not a phrase coined for this scene alone.

BLASPHEMY AGAINST THE HOLY SPIRIT (UNFORGIVABLE SIN)

The warning that speaking against the Holy Spirit `will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come' (12:31-32), delivered immediately after the Pharisees attribute Jesus's exorcism to Beelzebul (12:24). In its own narrative setting, the plainest referent is that specific accusation — naming the Spirit's visibly good work demonic — rather than any and every doubt or blasphemous outburst a later reader might fear qualifies [215]. The passage nonetheless generated substantial, long-running religious anxiety across Christian history; Augustine devoted a full sermon to resolving it as persistent, unrepentant hardness of heart rather than any single spoken sentence, a reading that eased one worry while opening a longer one about how a person could know whether they had crossed that line [214].

CAESAREA PHILIPPI

The setting of Peter's confession (Matthew 16:13–20) and one of the best-corroborated place-names in the entire Gospel record. The site is Banias (an Arabic corruption of its ancient name, Paneas/Panias), at the base of Mount Hermon, where the Hermon River rises from a spring inside a natural cave in a rock cliff.

The cave and spring had been a shrine to the god Pan since at least the Hellenistic period — votive niches cut into the cliff face date to around 200 BCE onward. Herod the Great built a temple to Augustus there, the "Augusteum"; Josephus describes it directly in Antiquities of the Jews 15.363–364, calling it "a temple of the whitest stone" built "near the place called Paneium," at the very cave and spring where the Jordan's headwaters rise. Herod's son Philip the Tetrarch subsequently rebuilt and expanded the site as his capital, renaming it Caesarea — with "Philippi" added to distinguish it from the coastal city Caesarea Maritima — around 2 BCE, exactly the city named in Matthew 16:13 and Mark 8:27.

Zvi Uri Ma'oz's Israel Antiquities Authority excavations of the terrace below the cliff, conducted 1988–1994 (published in Excavations and Surveys in Israel, vols. 13 and 15, Israel Antiquities Authority), uncovered the sequence of shrines, temples, and courtyards Josephus describes, in the exact location he places them relative to the cave and spring. This is a rare instance in Gospel geography where text, place-name history, and archaeology align without contradiction or gap.

Cited in: Matthew (beat covering 16:13).

CAIAPHAS

High priest of Jerusalem's Temple from 18 to 36 CE — one of the longest tenures of any 1st-century high priest, spanning the whole of Jesus's adult ministry and almost exactly matching Pontius Pilate's own prefecture (see PONTIUS PILATE). Matthew 26:3 places the chief priests and elders gathering "unto the palace of the high priest, who was called Caiaphas" to plot Jesus's arrest; he presides over the nighttime hearing described in 26:57–68.

Caiaphas's full name, per Josephus (Jewish Antiquities 18.35, 18.95) — who records his appointment by the Roman prefect Valerius Gratus and his removal by the Syrian legate Vitellius in roughly the same purge that recalled Pilate — was Joseph, called Caiaphas. In November 1990, a construction crew working in Jerusalem's Peace Forest (North Talpiot neighborhood) uncovered a burial cave; the Israel Antiquities Authority sent archaeologist Zvi Greenhut to excavate it, and among twelve ossuaries recovered, one — an elaborately decorated limestone bone box holding the remains of a man about 60 years old — carries a twice-repeated Aramaic inscription read as "Yehosef bar Qayafa" ("Joseph, son of Caiaphas"; Reich, R. (1992). Ossuary inscriptions from the "Caiaphas" tomb. 'Atiqot, 21, 72–77, is the initial scholarly publication). The inscription's match to Josephus's full name for the high priest is treated by most archaeologists as very likely — though not absolutely certain, since "Caiaphas" was a family name that could belong to a relative rather than the high priest himself — physical confirmation that a man named in both the Gospels and Josephus existed and was buried in Jerusalem. The ossuary is held at the Israel Museum, Jerusalem.

Cited in: Matthew 26:3, 26:57–68.

CAMEL THROUGH THE EYE OF A NEEDLE (HYPERBOLE, NOT A GATE)

The proverb at Matthew 19:24 — it being easier for a camel to pass through a needle's eye than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven — is popularly explained via a supposed small Jerusalem gate nicknamed 'the needle's eye,' through which an unloaded, kneeling camel could just barely pass. That gate has no ancient attestation of any kind; the legend is traceable only to a medieval gloss, associated with either the Byzantine commentator Theophylact or Anselm of Canterbury, later carried forward through Thomas Aquinas's Catena Aurea [155]. The saying is much better read as genuine, deliberately impossible hyperbole — the largest land animal a Palestinian audience knew set against the smallest common household opening, the same rhetorical mode already seen in this book's 'log in your own eye' discussion at chapter 7 [43]. The disciples' shocked response one verse later, 'who then can be saved?' (19:25), only makes sense if the image was meant as genuinely impossible, not merely difficult.

CANAANITE WOMAN VS. SYROPHOENICIAN WOMAN (MATTHEW VS. MARK NAMING)

The unnamed mother who pleads with Jesus on behalf of her demon-afflicted daughter in the district of Tyre and Sidon (15:21-28), called 'a Canaanite woman' by Matthew (15:22) but 'a Gentile, a Syrophoenician by birth' by Mark's version of the same encounter (Mark 7:26). 'Canaanite' had not been a live first-century ethnic self-designation, unlike Mark's contemporary administrative label; commentary treats Matthew's choice as a deliberate reach back into Israel's own scriptural vocabulary for its ancestral 'other,' a traceable editorial difference between the two Gospels rather than a claim about what she was actually called by her own community [243].

CAPERNAUM

The fishing village on the Sea of Galilee's north shore that Matthew 4:13 names as the base Jesus moved to after leaving Nazareth. Its location is not in dispute: the site is identified with Tell Hum (preserved in the modern Arabic name, a corruption of the Hebrew Kfar Nahum, "village of Nahum"), and the identification is old, uncontroversial, and unchallenged by any competing candidate site — a contrast with Bethsaida, below.

Franciscan archaeologists Virgilio Corbo and Stanislao Loffreda excavated the site's western half from 1968 onward, publishing the primary excavation report as Corbo, V. C. (1975), Cafarnao I: Gli edifici della città (Studium Biblicum Franciscanum, Collectio Maior 19a, Franciscan Printing Press, Jerusalem). Their dig uncovered an ornate white-limestone synagogue and, beneath its floor, tens of thousands of coins that dated the visible structure to the 4th or 5th century CE — centuries later than the "Galilee-type" 2nd–3rd century date Israeli scholars had argued for on stylistic grounds alone. Jodi Magness's later ceramic analysis, "The Pottery from the Village of Capernaum and the Chronology of Galilean Synagogues" (Tel Aviv, 39, 2012, pp. 238–250), reinforced the late dating and argued several other Galilean synagogues assigned to the 2nd–3rd century belong to the 4th–6th century instead.

Both excavators suspected the limestone building's basalt substructure was the wall of an earlier building — possibly an earlier synagogue on the same footprint, conceivably first-century. But the synagogue standing at Capernaum today, the one visitors are shown, was not the building Jesus taught in (Mark 1:21). The site is right; the surviving structure on it is not the same one.

Cited in: Matthew (beat covering 4:13).

CENTURION (ROMAN VS. HERODIAN MILITARY OFFICER)

A Greco-Roman military rank, roughly a company commander over about a hundred soldiers, held by the officer whose servant Jesus heals at a distance in Capernaum (8:5-13). English translations render the figure simply as a 'centurion,' inviting the assumption that he served in a literal Roman legion; but Galilee was governed by the client tetrarch Herod Antipas, not directly by Rome, until 44 CE, and Antipas is independently documented fielding his own locally raised forces organized and titled along Roman lines [158] [159]. The rank title 'centurion' was routinely adopted wholesale by client-king armies across the region, so the office does not by itself prove Roman citizenship or a Roman chain of command [160].

CHORAZIN

One of three towns Jesus condemns for failing to repent despite witnessing his miracles (Matthew 11:21, paralleled in Luke 10:13), alongside Bethsaida and Capernaum. The site is real and identified without serious dispute: Korazim National Park, Israel, roughly two miles north of Capernaum, on the basalt plateau above the Sea of Galilee.

Ze'ev Yeivin directed excavations at the site for Israel's Department of Antiquities in 1962–1964, resumed 1980–1987, publishing the final report as The Synagogue at Korazim: The 1962–1964, 1980–1987 Excavations (Israel Antiquities Authority Reports, 2000). The excavation uncovered an elaborately carved black basalt synagogue and surrounding town remains covering roughly 25 acres across five quarters.

As with Capernaum, the surviving synagogue building postdates the Gospel-era events it is associated with by a wide margin: construction is dated to the late 3rd or 4th century CE, with earthquake destruction and a later (6th-century) rebuilding — meaning the structure standing at Chorazin today is centuries removed from anything Jesus could have seen there, even though the settlement itself, and its real presence on Jesus's circuit, are not in question.

Cited in: Matthew (beat covering 11:21); see BETHSAIDA, CAPERNAUM.

CORBAN (VOW-LAW LOOPHOLE)

The Aramaic/Hebrew term for a vow dedicating property or support 'to God,' cited by Jesus as a real, documented halakhic mechanism some used to declare resources unavailable to support their own parents, in technical tension with the commandment to honor father and mother (15:5-6). The Mishnah's tractate Nedarim regulates this exact category of vow law in detail [241], and an inscribed first-century Jerusalem-area ossuary independently confirms the vocabulary was in genuine contemporary use, not an invented rhetorical target [242].

CRITERION OF DISSIMILARITY

A method used in historical-Jesus scholarship for weighing the likely authenticity of a saying or action attributed to Jesus: material is judged a stronger candidate for going back to Jesus himself when it does not closely resemble either the surrounding Judaism of his own day or the concerns of the later church that transmitted the Gospels, on the reasoning that such material is less likely to have been supplied by either side. First formulated by Ernst Kasemann in a 1953 lecture later published in his Essays on New Testament Themes [151], and applied since by scholars including John P. Meier [152] and E. P. Sanders [153] to features such as Jesus's unmediated, non-citational teaching authority in the Sermon on the Mount (7:21-23, 7:28-29). Related to, but methodologically distinct from, the criterion of embarrassment, which weighs material the early church would have had reason to suppress rather than material that simply lacks a clear precedent.

CRITERION OF EMBARRASSMENT

A tool of historical-Jesus scholarship, formalized in John P. Meier's A Marginal Jew project: a detail that would have been awkward or theologically inconvenient for the early church to invent is judged more likely to be historically genuine, on the reasoning that a movement shaping its own founding story has every incentive to omit or soften such details rather than manufacture them. First applied in this book to Jesus's baptism by John [16]; applied a second time to Peter's threefold denial of Jesus, a scene independently preserved across all four canonical Gospels despite naming the movement's most prominent later leader as its failure [356].

CYRENE

A Greek-founded city in Cyrenaica, on the coast of what is now eastern Libya. Matthew 27:32 names "a man of Cyrene, Simon by name" as the passerby Roman soldiers compel to carry Jesus's cross; Mark 15:21 adds that this Simon was "the father of Alexander and Rufus," implying his sons were known, presumably Christian, figures to Mark's first audience.

Cyrene's Jewish population by the 1st century was substantial and well documented, not a marginal or invented detail. Josephus (Against Apion, Book 2) records that Ptolemy I Soter (reigned 304–282 BCE) deliberately settled Jews in Cyrene and other Libyan cities to strengthen his hold on the region. He also preserves, in Antiquities of the Jews, Book 14, the Greek geographer Strabo's description of Cyrene's population as of roughly 85 BCE, divided into four recognized classes: citizens, farmers, resident aliens, and Jews — meaning Jews were an acknowledged, sizable civic category there generations before Jesus's lifetime. The book of Acts independently corroborates an active Cyrenian Jewish presence specifically in Jerusalem: Acts 2:10 lists visitors "from the parts of Libya belonging to Cyrene" among the Pentecost crowd, and Acts 6:9 names a "synagogue of the Freedmen," made up in part of Cyrenians and Alexandrians, operating in the city.

A tentative, unproven archaeological correlate exists. In November 1941, archaeologist Eleazar Sukenik excavated a Jewish burial cave in Jerusalem's Kidron Valley, pre-dating 70 CE, containing an ossuary inscribed twice in Greek with the name "Alexander son of Simon." Sukenik himself raised, cautiously, the possibility of a connection to Mark's Alexander and Simon; his own excavation assistant, Nahman Avigad, expressed doubt about the identification in his full 1962 publication of the tomb in the Israel Exploration Journal — the name pairing is common enough that certainty isn't warranted, only a suggestive coincidence worth naming honestly as unconfirmed.

Whatever the ossuary's status, the larger point stands independent of it: a Cyrenian Jew present in Jerusalem for Passover in the early 1st century, exactly as Matthew 27:32 describes, fits a documented, decades-old pattern of diaspora pilgrimage from a real, sizable, independently-attested Jewish community — it requires no special explanation to be plausible.

Cited in: Matthew 27:32

DANIEL

Daniel appears in Matthew only once, at 24:15 — "when ye therefore shall see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet" — part of Jesus's Olivet Discourse on the destruction of the Temple; Mark's parallel to this same passage (13:14) omits Daniel's name entirely, referring only to "the abomination of desolation" without attribution.

The book of Daniel presents itself as written by a Jewish courtier living through the Babylonian exile and the early Persian period, roughly the 6th century BCE. Critical scholarship, however, holds a near-consensus view that the book's visionary chapters (7-12) were actually composed some four centuries later, during the Seleucid persecution of Judea under Antiochus IV Epiphanes in the 160s BCE. The clearest evidence for this is internal: Daniel 11 narrates the wars of the Hellenistic successor kingdoms in extraordinarily precise, accurate detail up through Antiochus IV's early reign, then shifts abruptly at verse 40 into vague and historically inaccurate predictions about his death — the seam most critical scholars identify as the boundary between ex eventu ("after the event") prophecy, written up as if predictive, and the author's own genuine, and mistaken, guess at what would happen next. John J. Collins, Daniel: A Commentary on the Book of Daniel (Hermeneia; Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 1993), is the standard critical treatment establishing this reading; the ex eventu observation itself dates back to the 3rd-century-CE philosopher Porphyry, whose critique (preserved secondhand through Jerome's commentary on Daniel) is usually credited as the earliest to notice the pattern.

For Matthew's single citation (24:15), the underlying dating debate does not change what Jesus is depicted as doing with the phrase: invoking "the abomination of desolation" as a known, named prophetic reference point for a future desolation of the Temple, regardless of when in Daniel's compositional history that phrase was actually written.

Cited in: Matthew 24:15.

DAUGHTER OF HERODIAS

The unnamed girl of Matthew 14:6–11 whose dance at Herod Antipas's birthday banquet pleases him enough that he swears to grant her any request; prompted by her mother Herodias, she asks for John the Baptist's head on a platter, and Antipas — reluctant per the text, but bound by his oath and unwilling to lose face before his guests — has it done. Matthew never names her, and neither does Mark's parallel version of the same episode (6:17–29).

The name "Salome" comes entirely from Josephus (Jewish Antiquities 18.136), not from either Gospel. Josephus records that Herodias's daughter by her first marriage (see HERODIAS) was named Salome, and that she was later married first to her step-great-uncle Philip the tetrarch (see PHILIP (HUSBAND OF HERODIAS)) and, after his death, to Aristobulus of Chalcis. Centuries of later tradition — most famously Oscar Wilde's play Salome (written 1891) and the operas and paintings it inspired — have fused Josephus's name onto the Gospel's dancing girl; the identification is widely accepted as most likely correct given how the family details line up, but it rests on combining two independent sources, since neither text names her in this scene itself.

This figure should not be confused with the disciple Salome named separately in Mark 15:40 and 16:1, one of the women present at the crucifixion and the empty tomb — an unrelated person who happens, in later tradition, to share the same name pulled from Josephus for Herodias's daughter.

Cited in: Matthew 14:6–11; see HEROD ANTIPAS, HERODIAS.

DAVID

Matthew's genealogy is built around him: he is the hinge of all three fourteen-generation spans (1:17), named explicitly in the opening verse ("the son of David," 1:1), and the reason Matthew's version of the line runs through Solomon rather than any of David's other sons (1:6) — establishing Jesus's legal claim to a Davidic, and therefore messianic, lineage (2 Samuel 7:12-16). In the Hebrew Bible's own account (1-2 Samuel, 1 Kings 1-2), David is a shepherd anointed king over a united Israel and Judah, conqueror of Jerusalem, and founder of a dynasty that, on the text's own terms, rules a substantial regional kingdom.

Two distinct questions get run together in popular discussion of David and need to be kept separate. First: did a King David, founder of a real dynasty, exist at all? This is the more settled of the two — the Tel Dan Stele, an Aramaic inscription fragment discovered by Avraham Biran and Joseph Naveh at Tel Dan in 1993 (published as "An Aramaic Stele Fragment from Tel Dan," Israel Exploration Journal 43, 1993), contains the phrase bytdwd, "House of David," referring to the ruling dynasty of Judah from the perspective of a hostile Aramean king roughly a century after David's traditional reign — the earliest and most widely accepted extra-biblical attestation that a "David" dynasty was a real, named political entity by the mid-9th century BCE. See Note 2 for the full treatment of the stele.

Second, and considerably more contested: what was the actual size and character of David's kingdom? Here the "United Monarchy" debate divides mainstream and minimalist scholarship. Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman's David and Solomon: In Search of the Bible's Sacred Kings and the Roots of the Western Tradition (Free Press, 2006) argues, building on Finkelstein's "Low Chronology" redating of Iron Age strata (Finkelstein, "The Archaeology of the United Monarchy: An Alternative View," Levant 28, 1996, pp. 177-187), that the archaeological record supports only a small hill-country chiefdom centered on Jerusalem, not the large, wealthy, administratively complex empire 1-2 Samuel and 1 Kings describe — with the grander biblical account read as a later, 7th-century Judahite retrojection. Traditionalist scholarship (see Kenneth Kitchen, On the Reliability of the Old Testament, Eerdmans, 2003, cited fully at Note 1) argues the archaeological gap reflects incomplete excavation and preservation bias rather than the kingdom's absence. The dynasty's existence and the kingdom's scale are, in short, two different claims with two different evidentiary standings — the first attested, the second still argued.

Cited in: Matthew 1:1, 1:6, 1:17; see Note 2.

DAY-LABORER HIRING MARKET (ROMAN-ERA MARKETPLACE)

The public gathering point the vineyard-workers parable assumes without explaining, where unemployed men waited each morning hoping a landowner or contractor would choose them for a day's paid work (20:1-7). This hiring-square practice is attested widely across Greco-Roman sources describing casual and agricultural labor, and Kenneth Bailey documents it as a custom still observable, in essentially the same form, in twentieth-century Middle Eastern towns [287]. The parable's setting is a real, checkable feature of the ancient Mediterranean labor economy, not an invented backdrop for the story.

DECAPOLIS

The "Ten Cities," a loose league of Greco-Roman urban centers mostly east of the Jordan, from which crowds follow Jesus per Matthew 4:25, alongside Galilee, Jerusalem, Judea, and the region beyond the Jordan. The league formed after Pompey's reorganization of the region in 63 BCE, folding formerly independent Hellenistic cities into a shared Roman administrative and cultural sphere.

Pliny the Elder's Natural History 5.74 (c. 77 CE; standard modern edition: Pliny, Natural History, Volume II: Books 3–7, H. Rackham, Trans., Loeb Classical Library, Harvard University Press, 1942) names the ten as Damascus, Philadelphia (modern Amman), Raphana, Scythopolis (Beth Shean, the only one west of the Jordan), Gadara, Hippos, Dion, Pella, Gerasa, and Canatha. All ten are real, located, and — with Gerasa and Scythopolis especially — extensively excavated, with well-preserved Roman colonnaded streets, theaters, and temples surviving at multiple sites today.

Membership and the exact list varied by source and period — Ptolemy's 2nd-century-CE geography names additional cities beyond Pliny's ten — and "league" is better understood as a shared urban-Hellenistic civic identity within a largely Semitic-speaking countryside than as a formally chartered political federation. But its general reality, membership, and location are not seriously disputed by any position on the spectrum.

Cited in: Matthew (beat covering 4:25).

DENARIUS (ROMAN DAY-LABORER WAGE)

The standard Roman silver coin paid to each vineyard worker in this chapter's opening parable, `whatever is right'' having already been fixed at one denarius for a full day's labor (20:2, 20:9-10, 20:13). This was the real, well-documented going rate for unskilled and casual agricultural labor across the first-century Roman world, not a figure invented to make the parable's math come out even: Tacitus records Roman soldiers citing a denarius a day as a recognized pay benchmark [284], Roman-era Egyptian payroll papyri independently document unskilled laborers earning in the same range [285], and the same figure recurs as a day's wage in the book of Tobit [286]. See also the tribute-penny denarius of Matthew 22:19-21, a separate scene involving the same coin denomination in a different context.

EARTHQUAKE AND RAISED SAINTS (MATTHEW 27:51-53)

The darkness, earthquake, and 'many bodies of the saints' raised at Jesus's death (27:51-53), unique to Matthew among the four Gospels and unattested in any independent contemporary source, already receives this book's fullest historical-critical treatment elsewhere [20]. The passage has also generated a notable controversy inside scholarship committed to defending Gospel historicity: Michael Licona's 2010 proposal that it functions as apocalyptic 'poetic device' rather than literal history drew a sharp public rebuttal from Norman Geisler and cost Licona a teaching post, before a theological journal convened scholars including Craig Blomberg to weigh the dispute directly [368] [369].

EGYPT

Matthew 2:13-15 has Joseph flee with Mary and the infant Jesus to Egypt to escape Herod, returning only after Herod's death. No independent Roman or Egyptian record of this specific family's journey survives — which is unsurprising rather than suspicious on its own terms: nothing about an obscure Judean family fleeing a local client king's paranoia would have registered with either Roman or Egyptian record-keeping of the period, which is exactly the kind of ordinary movement of ordinary people no ancient bureaucracy tracked.

What is independently well documented is that Egypt was a real, plausible refuge destination, because established Jewish communities were already there. Alexandria held one of the largest Jewish diaspora populations anywhere in the ancient world by the 1st century CE, described from the inside by the contemporary Jewish philosopher Philo of Alexandria and surveyed in detail by modern scholarship (John M. G. Barclay, Jews in the Mediterranean Diaspora: From Alexander to Trajan (323 BCE-117 CE), T&T Clark, 1996). Egyptian Jewish settlement went back centuries further still: the Elephantine papyri document a Jewish military garrison stationed at Elephantine, on Egypt's southern frontier, as early as the 5th century BCE, complete with its own temple and correspondence with authorities in Jerusalem (Bezalel Porten, Archives from Elephantine: The Life of an Ancient Jewish Military Colony, University of California Press, 1968).

Set against that backdrop, Matthew's flight-to-Egypt account describes a journey to a real, populated, historically continuous Jewish diaspora region — not an implausible destination — even though the specific family's trip leaves no trace of its own outside Matthew's text.

Cited in: Matthew 2:13

ELIJAH

Referenced by Jesus at Matthew 11:14 — "and if you are willing to accept it, he [John the Baptist] is the Elijah who is to come" — and, like Moses, given rare bodily presence at the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:1-13), appearing beside Moses in the vision on the mountain. Elijah is the only Hebrew Bible figure the Gospels treat as a live, still-pending expectation rather than a closed historical episode, which is what makes both mentions unusual.

That expectation has a specific scriptural origin. 2 Kings 2:11 describes Elijah taken up "in a whirlwind" by "a chariot of fire and horses of fire" rather than dying an ordinary death — the one Hebrew Bible figure, alongside Enoch (Genesis 5:24), whose story avoids a stated death. Malachi 4:5 (numbered 3:23 in the Hebrew Bible/Jewish Publication Society tradition) then prophesies that God "will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and terrible day of the LORD" — a return, not a resurrection, since by this reading Elijah never actually died. This is the expectation Matthew 11:14 draws on directly.

The Gospels do not agree among themselves on how to resolve it. Matthew 11:14 identifies John the Baptist as that returning Elijah, and Matthew 17:10-13 has Jesus tell Peter, James, and John after the Transfiguration that "Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him," glossing this again as John. John 1:21, however, has the Baptist asked directly, "Are you Elijah?" and answer, "I am not." Raymond E. Brown's *An Introduction to the New Testament* (Doubleday, 1997) discusses this identification as one of the points where the Synoptic tradition and the Johannine tradition present the Baptist's self-understanding differently rather than in simple harmony — a genuine internal disagreement among the four Gospels about who, if anyone, fulfills Malachi's prophecy, left visible here rather than resolved.

Elijah's appearance at the Transfiguration carries the same evidentiary limit noted for Moses (see MOSES): a private scene, attested only within the Gospel tradition itself, with the one explicit outside claim of eyewitness testimony (2 Peter 1:16-18) coming from a letter mainstream scholarship dates late and regards as written under a false name. Whether Elijah appeared is not a question the independent record can speak to either way.

Cited in: Matthew (beat covering 11:2-15; beat covering 17:1-13)

ESSENES

A first-century Jewish sect described by the contemporary historian Flavius Josephus, closely associated by most scholars (though not identical by name) with the wilderness community that produced the Dead Sea Scrolls at Qumran. Josephus records that the Essenes avoided oath-swearing in ordinary speech as a matter of communal principle, holding their plain word to be as binding as any oath — a genuine, independently attested first-century Jewish parallel to Jesus's own blanket prohibition on oath-taking in this chapter (5:33-37), while the Essenes still required solemn oaths of initiates joining the community [123].

FIG TREE (PROPHETIC JUDGMENT SYMBOL)

The tree Jesus curses for bearing no fruit (21:18-22), read by mainstream scholarship not as an isolated nature miracle but as an enacted version of an established Old Testament prophetic image — fruitless fig trees and vines standing for a nation found wanting under judgment, already present in Jeremiah 8:13, Hosea 9:10, and Micah 7:1 [300]. A dedicated redaction-critical study of the scene argues it functions as a symbolic indictment of the Temple establishment specifically, staged around the Temple action rather than reported as a separate incident [299].

FIRST-CENTURY GALILEAN FISHING ECONOMY

The regulated, capital-intensive trade the first four disciples are drawn from in this chapter (4:18-22): fishing on the Sea of Galilee under Herod Antipas required leased or licensed lake access and real investment in boats and nets, and larger family operations employed hired labor beyond immediate relatives [107]. Mark's parallel account of the same calling scene notes that Zebedee, father of James and John, retained 'hired servants' in his boat after his sons departed, a detail Matthew's own version does not include, but one that situates the family's operation as a business of some substance rather than bare subsistence [108].

GALILEE

The northern region of Roman-era Palestine, containing Nazareth and the Sea of Galilee, and — after Herod the Great's death — the tetrarchy of his son Herod Antipas (4 BCE-39 CE), governed separately from Judea to its south for this entire span.

That distinction matters directly for Matthew 2:22: after Herod's death, Joseph is warned in a dream against returning to Judea specifically because Archelaus now reigns there, and withdraws instead to Galilee. This makes real administrative sense rather than being an arbitrary narrative choice. Judea under Archelaus remained the more closely watched former royal seat, and within a decade would become a directly Roman-governed province after his deposal in 6 CE, while Galilee stayed under a separate, longer-lasting client tetrarch whose rule was comparatively stable for most of Jesus's lifetime (Sean Freyne, Galilee from Alexander the Great to Hadrian, 323 B.C.E. to 135 C.E.: A Study of Second Temple Judaism, University of Notre Dame Press/Michael Glazier, 1980). Galilee and Judea were never merged administratively in this period; a family relocating from one to the other was moving between two genuinely different Roman client arrangements, not simply changing address within one government's reach.

Cited in: Matthew 2:22

GEMATRIA (NUMERICAL VALUE OF NAMES)

The Hebrew and Greek practice of computing a numerical value for a word or name from its own letters, each of which also served as a numeral in a period before either language had a separate number-writing system. Matthew's genealogy (1:1-17) organizes itself into three sets of exactly fourteen generations, and fourteen is the sum of the Hebrew consonants in David's own name — dalet-vav-dalet, four plus six plus four [67]. Recounting Matthew's own third set of names (1:12-16) yields only thirteen entries unless one name is counted twice, a shortfall long noted and never resolved by the text itself.

GENNESARET

The fertile plain running along the Sea of Galilee's northwestern shore, between Capernaum and Tiberias — real, geographically uncontested, and the landing point Matthew 14:34 (paralleled at Mark 6:53) gives for Jesus's boat after the walking-on-water episode.

Josephus, an independent, contemporary, non-Christian source with direct familiarity with the region (he commanded Galilee's defenses during the Jewish revolt), gives an extended, admiring description of the plain in Jewish War 3.10.8 (Thackeray translation, Loeb Classical Library, Harvard University Press, 1927): he calls it "wonderful in its nature and beauty," noting that its soil and climate somehow support walnut trees (which need cold), palms (which need heat), and figs and olives (which need a temperate climate) all growing side by side — a genuine independent corroboration not just that the plain existed, but of its specific reputation for exceptional agricultural fertility in exactly this period.

Cited in: Matthew (beat covering 14:34); see SEA OF GALILEE.

GETHSEMANE

A garden at the foot of the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron Valley from Jerusalem, where Matthew places Jesus's final prayer and arrest (26:36-56). The name is generally derived from Hebrew/Aramaic for "oil press," consistent with its setting among cultivated olive groves rather than naming anything more symbolically loaded.

The traditional site is marked today by the Church of All Nations (also called the Basilica of the Agony), built in the 1920s and in Franciscan custody of the surrounding grove since 1681. Within its garden stand eight olive trees of genuinely striking age and girth, long promoted to visitors — including by some tourism and pilgrimage literature — as the very trees under which Jesus prayed. That specific claim does not hold up: a 2015 dendrochronological and radiocarbon study by Italian researcher Mauro Bernabei, published in the Journal of Archaeological Science (vol. 53, pp. 43-48), was able to successfully core and date only three of the eight trees (the others are hollow at the center, where the oldest wood would be, making direct dating impossible); all three dated samples returned ages placing their origin in the 12th century CE, during the Crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem — roughly eleven hundred years too late to have existed in the 1st century, though genuinely ancient by any ordinary standard and plausibly among the oldest cultivated olive trees on record.

This is a clean small-scale example of legendary accretion: a real, geographically plausible site (the general location at the foot of the Mount of Olives is not disputed) accumulating a specific, emotionally resonant physical detail — these exact trees — that the physical evidence itself does not support, likely because a medieval planting was mistaken, understandably, for continuous survival from antiquity.

Cited in: Matthew 26:36.

GIFT MIRACLE (FORM-CRITICAL CATEGORY)

A form-critical classification, distinct from healing and exorcism accounts, for miracle stories in which Jesus unexpectedly and without request supplies a specific material need, narrated with no interest in the mechanism of provision [264]. The fish-with-a-coin story of Matthew 17:24-27 is a clear instance, appearing only in Matthew with no Synoptic or Johannine parallel and a distinctly folkloric narrative texture compared to surrounding healing material [266]; Elisha's Old Testament provision miracles (2 Kings 4:1-7, 4:42-44) supply a form-critical ancestor for the same basic story shape [265], and this Gospel's own feeding-miracle doublet [247] belongs to the same category.

GOLDEN RULE (CROSS-CULTURAL ATTESTATION)

The reciprocity principle stated positively in Matthew 7:12 ("whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them") and attested, mostly in negative form, across a range of ancient ethical traditions predating or independent of the Gospels. Confirmed close parallels cited in this chapter include Hillel the Elder's negative formulation recorded in the Babylonian Talmud (Shabbat 31a) [141], the deuterocanonical Book of Tobit (4:15), dated roughly two centuries before Jesus [142], Confucius's Analects (15.23), five centuries earlier still and from an entirely separate tradition [143], and the Athenian rhetorician Isocrates's Nicocles (61) [144]. Mainstream critical commentary treats the convergence as genuine, independent ethical convergence rather than either borrowing or coincidence [145].

GOLGOTHA

Aramaic/Hebrew for "place of the skull" (rendered into Latin as Calvaria, source of the English "Calvary"), the site of the crucifixion in all four Gospels (Matthew 27:33). Two different traditional locations compete for the honor, and neither can be archaeologically proven to be the exact spot.

The older and more widely held candidate is the site beneath the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, inside Jerusalem's Old City today but plausibly outside the city walls in the 1st century — a distinction that matters, since Roman and Jewish practice both placed execution and burial sites outside inhabited city limits. Excavations conducted under and around the church across the 1960s-1970s by the Franciscan archaeologist Fr. Virgilio Corbo (published as Il Santo Sepolcro di Gerusalemme, Aspetti Archeologici dalle origini al periodo crociato, Parts I-III, Franciscan Printing Press, Jerusalem, 1981-1982) documented an ancient stone quarry, abandoned and repurposed as a garden-cemetery, containing rock-cut tombs of the correct 1st-century style — physical confirmation that the area functioned as an extramural burial ground consistent with the Gospels' own claims (a garden, John 19:41; near but outside the city, John 19:20; cf. Hebrews 13:12), even though the identification of this exact rock outcrop with Golgotha itself rests on a continuous tradition traced back only to the 4th century, when Bishop Eusebius and the Emperor Constantine's building program identified the site during the construction of the original church.

The rival candidate is the "Garden Tomb," a rock-cut tomb north of the Old City walls near a skull-like rock formation, discovered in 1867 and popularized in 1883 by the British general Charles George Gordon, who argued it was the true, more visually evocative Calvary against what he considered a compromised, over-built traditional site. Archaeological study of the tomb itself has since dated its burial style to the First Temple period — centuries before Jesus — making it, on the evidence, too old to be the "new tomb" the Gospels describe (Matthew 27:60; John 19:41). The Holy Sepulchre site accordingly carries both the older continuous tradition and the stronger archaeological case, without either point amounting to proof of the exact spot.

Cited in: Matthew 27:33.

GOMORRAH

Gomorrah has no independent narrative of its own in scripture — it is named only ever paired with Sodom, as its co-destroyed twin (Genesis 19; Deuteronomy 29:23; Isaiah 1:9–10; Matthew 10:15), which is itself worth noting as a feature of the text rather than an oversight of this entry.

The same archaeological-identification question raised at SODOM applies here without a separate body of evidence. Numeira, the smaller Early Bronze Age site excavated (alongside Bab edh-Dhra) by Walter E. Rast and R. Thomas Schaub from the 1970s onward, is the standard proposed match for Gomorrah under the "southern cities of the plain" hypothesis — a real settlement with a documented violent destruction (burned structures, ash, collapse) dated to roughly 2350–2300 BCE, at the end of Early Bronze III. As with Bab edh-Dhra/Sodom, no inscription at Numeira confirms the name "Gomorrah," and the destruction date runs several centuries earlier than traditional patriarchal-era chronology would place the Genesis 19 narrative — so the identification carries the same open, unresolved status: a plausible, geographically apt candidate, not a proven one.

Referenced at Matthew 10:15, alongside the dust-shaking instruction covered in Chapter 10; this book does not separately discuss the Sodom/Gomorrah comparison itself. See SODOM.

GOSPEL AUTHORSHIP (TRADITIONAL ATTRIBUTION VS. CRITICAL SCHOLARSHIP)

The question of who actually wrote the Gospel bearing Matthew's name, raised directly by his calling in this chapter (9:9; see MATTHEW (LEVI)). The earliest external testimony, a fragment of Papias of Hierapolis preserved by Eusebius of Caesarea, describes Matthew compiling sayings `in the Hebrew dialect'' [171], a description that does not match the finished Gospel's polished, Mark-dependent Greek composition [173]. Mainstream critical scholarship concludes the Gospel was written by a later, unknown author working in Matthew's name and tradition, not by the apostle himself [174]; a smaller traditional and evangelical position argues for an authentic apostolic core beneath the finished text [175]. See PAPIAS OF HIERAPOLIS.

GREAT COMMISSION (TRINITARIAN FORMULA'S TEXTUAL HISTORY)

The baptismal instruction closing the Great Commission — "baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (28:19) — distinct from this book's existing entry on the mission's widening geographic scope (see ISRAEL-FIRST MISSION VS. GREAT COMMISSION). Every baptism actually narrated in Acts instead uses a simpler, Jesus-only formula (Acts 2:38; 8:16; 10:48; 19:5), a gap mainstream scholarship reads as evidence the fuller triadic wording reflects Matthew's own later liturgical practice [375]. No manuscript of Matthew lacks the triadic reading, and an independent early Christian text, the Didache, already uses the same three-part formula on its own [376].

GREAT ISAIAH SCROLL (1QISA^A)

The oldest complete surviving copy of the biblical Book of Isaiah, one of the original Dead Sea Scrolls recovered from Qumran Cave 1 in 1947 and paleographically dated to roughly the 2nd century BCE. At Isaiah 7:14 it reads the Hebrew ha-almah, identical to the wording later preserved in the medieval Masoretic Text, confirming that reading was already fixed more than a century before Jesus's birth and could not have been altered afterward in reaction to Christian claims about a virgin birth [69]. Housed today in the Shrine of the Book, Israel Museum, Jerusalem.

GUARD AT THE TOMB (MATTHEW'S UNIQUE APOLOGETIC)

The sequence — a guard requested from Pilate (27:62-66), terrified soldiers, and a bribe to say the disciples stole the body (28:11-15) — found only in Matthew among the four canonical Gospels, closing with Matthew's own concession that the rival stolen-body explanation "has been spread among the Jews to this day" (28:15) [370]. The word for the guard itself, koustodia, leaves genuinely open whether Roman or Temple personnel are meant [371]. The rival explanation Matthew answers is independently attested still circulating a century later in Justin Martyr [372], and resurfaces, reworked, centuries further on in the medieval Toledot Yeshu tradition [373].

HEROD ANTIPAS

Another son of Herod the Great, by Malthace — full brother of Archelaus (see ARCHELAUS) — and, unlike his brother, given the lesser title tetrarch when their father's kingdom was divided in 4 BCE: he ruled Galilee and Perea, not Judea, for the whole of Jesus's adult ministry. Matthew 14:1 introduces him as "Herod the tetrarch," hearing reports of Jesus and wondering if this is John the Baptist "risen from the dead" — the same Herod who, per Matthew 14:3–11, had John arrested and beheaded at a birthday banquet, in an account entangled with his wife Herodias and her daughter (see HERODIAS; DAUGHTER OF HERODIAS). Luke's Gospel separately has Jesus call him "that fox" (Luke 13:32), a warning relayed to Jesus that Herod wants him dead.

Josephus (Jewish Antiquities 18.116–119) independently confirms Antipas executed John the Baptist but gives a different proximate cause than the Gospels: not the banquet oath, but political calculation — John's enormous popular following, in Josephus's telling, worried Antipas that "the great crowds that seemed ready to do anything he should advise" might tip into rebellion, so he had John imprisoned and killed preemptively at the fortress of Machaerus, near the Dead Sea. Josephus and the Gospels agree on the outcome and disagree on the dramatized motive — a pattern comparable to the Pilate trial narrative (see PONTIUS PILATE), where an independent source confirms the bare fact and the Gospel supplies theatrical detail the outside record doesn't corroborate.

Antipas's reign ended without any Gospel event: in 39 CE, per Josephus (Jewish Antiquities 18.240–252), his nephew Herod Agrippa I — recently made king by the emperor Caligula — denounced him as disloyal and militarily overreaching, citing a weapons stockpile Josephus says was sufficient for 70,000 men. Caligula stripped Antipas of his title and territory and exiled him to Lugdunum in Gaul (identified by most historians with modern Lyon, though Josephus's separate account in Jewish War gives the exile location as Spain instead — an unresolved discrepancy between his own two books). Herodias, offered the chance to keep her own property separately as Agrippa's sister, chose exile with her husband instead.

Cited in: Matthew 14:1, 14:3–11; see HERODIAS, DAUGHTER OF HERODIAS.

HEROD II (HERODIAS'S FIRST HUSBAND)

The son of Herod the Great and Mariamne II (daughter of the high priest Simon Boethus) whom Herodias actually married first, before leaving him for his half-brother Herod Antipas — named plainly as "Herod," never "Philip," by the independent historian Flavius Josephus [227]. Modern historians call him Herod II purely to distinguish him from his father and his many half-brothers who also carried the name Herod; he held no tetrarchy or territorial title of his own, unlike Philip the tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis (see PHILIP (HUSBAND OF HERODIAS)), a genuinely separate figure the Gospels' single word "Philip" conflates him with. Harold Hoehner's standard scholarly reconstruction of the Herodian family tree treats this conflation as the likely product of the family's own habit of reusing the names Herod and Philip across half-brothers by different mothers [226], a confusion the manuscript tradition itself partly reflects: a number of early manuscripts of Matthew 14:3 and its Markan parallel omit the name "Philip" altogether [228].

Cited in: Matthew 14:3; see HERODIAS, PHILIP (HUSBAND OF HERODIAS), HEROD ANTIPAS.

HEROD THE GREAT

King of Judea under Rome from 37 BCE until his death — nominated "king of the Jews" by the Roman Senate in 40 BCE on Mark Antony's recommendation, but a client king, not an independent monarch. Matthew's nativity places Jesus's birth "in the days of Herod the king" (2:1); Herod appears consulting his own priests and scribes about the Messiah's birthplace, then (2:16–18) ordering the killing of Bethlehem's boys age two and under after the Magi fail to report back — the "Slaughter of the Innocents."

Herod's reign is independently and extensively documented by Josephus (Jewish Antiquities 15–17; Jewish War 1), whose account of Herod's later years is dominated by an escalating brutality inside his own household: he had his wife Mariamne executed on suspicion of infidelity and conspiracy (Antiquities 15.7.4–6, c. 29 BCE), and, in his final years, three of his own sons — Alexander, Aristobulus, and Antipater (Antiquities 16.11, 17.7) — on the same charge. The Roman writer Macrobius (Saturnalia 2.4.11, early 5th century CE, drawing on earlier material) preserves a joke attributed to Augustus on hearing of one of these killings — "it is better to be Herod's pig (hus) than his son (huios)," a pun on the fact that Herod, keeping Jewish dietary law, would never eat the one but had killed several of the other — already circulating as commentary on this reputation in antiquity. Alongside the family violence, Herod was also the era's most ambitious builder in the region: the Temple Mount's expansion in Jerusalem, the desert fortress at Masada, and the artificial harbor city of Caesarea Maritima are all his construction, and substantial remains of all three still stand (Richardson, P. (1996). Herod: King of the Jews and friend of the Romans. University of South Carolina Press, is the standard modern biography weighing both the brutality and the building program together).

Josephus dates Herod's death (Antiquities 17.6.4, 17.9.3) to shortly after a lunar eclipse and before that year's Passover — scholarly consensus places this in early 4 BCE (a minority view argues 1 BCE), meaning Matthew's own chronology requires Jesus to have been born before the era later named for his birth even begins. What has no independent corroboration at all is the Bethlehem massacre itself: no source outside Matthew — not Josephus, who documents Herod's other cruelties in detail, not any Roman historian — records it, which is the main reason critical scholars read the episode as Matthew's own composition, patterned on Exodus's Pharaoh-versus-Hebrew-infants story, rather than an attested event.

Cited in: Matthew 2:1, 2:3–9, 2:16–18; see ARCHELAUS.

HERODIANS (POLITICAL FACTION)

A real, if imprecisely documented, political faction named alongside the Pharisees in Matthew 22:16, and elsewhere in Mark (3:6, 12:13), generally understood by historians as a loose network of loyalists to Herodian rule rather than a formally organized sect on the order of the Pharisees or Sadducees. Matthew's own Gospel names the group only here, having dropped it from his parallel to Mark 3:6 (Matthew 12:14) and substituted 'the Sadducees' for it in his version of Mark's leaven warning (Matthew 16:6) — a checkable pattern in how this Gospel handled its source material [303].

HERODIAS

Granddaughter of Herod the Great through his executed son Aristobulus (see HEROD THE GREAT), and, per Matthew 14:3, the wife Herod Antipas took from "Philip his brother" — a marriage John the Baptist publicly condemned as unlawful (14:4, echoing Leviticus 18:16/20:21's prohibition on marrying a brother's wife), which the Gospel presents as her motive for wanting John dead.

Josephus (Jewish Antiquities 18.109–115, 136) is the independent source for her actual family history, and it complicates Matthew's single sentence: Herodias's first husband was not the "Philip" of Luke 3:1 (Philip the tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis, a different son of Herod the Great, by a different mother) but another son, whom Josephus calls simply "Herod" — a half-brother of Antipas by Mariamne II, daughter of the high priest Simon — referred to by modern historians as Herod II to distinguish him from his father and his many half-brothers also named Herod. It was this Herod II, not Philip the tetrarch, whom Herodias left to marry Antipas; the Gospels' naming of her first husband as "Philip" is very likely a conflation with the better-known Philip of Luke 3:1, an error most scholars trace to Mark (the shared source behind Matthew's version) rather than to any competing historical tradition (see PHILIP).

When Antipas was denounced to Caligula and stripped of his tetrarchy in 39 CE (see HEROD ANTIPAS), Josephus records that Caligula offered to let Herodias, as Agrippa I's sister, keep her own property and status apart from her disgraced husband — and that she refused, choosing exile with Antipas instead, a decision Josephus treats as a genuine point in her favor.

Cited in: Matthew 14:3–4; see HEROD ANTIPAS, PHILIP (HUSBAND OF HERODIAS), DAUGHTER OF HERODIAS.

HILLEL THE ELDER

A leading Pharisaic sage active in Jerusalem in the decades before and around the turn of the era, traditionally dated to roughly 110 BCE-10 CE — a real, datable figure whose teaching activity predates Jesus's own ministry by a generation or so. He is remembered, in a story first written down centuries later in the Babylonian Talmud, for summarizing the whole Torah for a prospective convert as "what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor," the closest and best-attested Jewish parallel to the positive Golden Rule of Matthew 7:12 [141]. Cited in this chapter for comparative purposes only; nothing here claims Matthew's Jesus knew or quoted Hillel directly.

HILLEL VS. SHAMMAI ON DIVORCE (LIVE HALAKHIC DEBATE)

The specific, named first-century rabbinic dispute over how broadly to read Deuteronomy 24:1's grounds for divorce — 'because he has found some indecency in her' — recorded in the Mishnah as a disagreement between the House of Hillel (broad: divorce permitted for almost any cause) and the House of Shammai (narrow: divorce permitted only for actual sexual misconduct) [273]. This is a distinct topic from Hillel's general ethical teaching already discussed in this book under HILLEL THE ELDER (the negative Golden Rule of Matthew 7:12); here Hillel and Shammai appear specifically as legal disputants, and Matthew's version of Jesus's divorce ruling situates him inside their live argument, closer to Shammai's stricter reading [274]. Mark and Luke's parallel versions of the same core teaching state the prohibition with no exception clause at all, a real difference from Matthew's text worth noting alongside this debate [277].

IMMANUEL INCLUSIO (MATTHEW 1:23 / 28:20)

The Gospel's closing line, "I am with you always, to the end of the age" (28:20), read by mainstream commentary as a deliberate inclusio answering the naming of Jesus as Emmanuel, "God with us," at the book's opening (1:23, quoting Isaiah 7:14), with a further echo sounded in between at 18:20 [380]. The same closing scene sets the Great Commission's "all authority" claim against Daniel 7:13-14's enthroned "son of man" [378], and its mountain setting against a sustained Mosaic mountain-typology running through the whole Gospel [379].

INNOCENT-BLOOD HAND-WASHING (DEUTERONOMY 21:6-9)

The Torah's own legal-ritual background for Pilate's hand-washing gesture at Matthew 27:24. Deuteronomy 21:6-9 provides a specific procedure for an unsolved murder: the elders of the nearest town break a heifer's neck in an unworked valley and wash their hands over it, declaring their hands did not shed the blood and their eyes did not see it — a formal disclaimer of responsibility for a killing the community cannot solve, addressed to God rather than a court [363]. Raymond Brown reads Matthew's Pilate as borrowing this exact form and inverting it: unlike Deuteronomy's elders, Pilate disclaims a killing he is, in the same scene, actively ordering and has the actual power to stop [364]. Distinct from NETILAT YADAYIM (RITUAL HAND-WASHING), which concerns ordinary pre-meal purity practice rather than a legal disclaimer of bloodguilt. See PONTIUS PILATE.

ISAAC

Abraham's son by his wife Sarah (Genesis 21:1-3), and the middle link of the three-generation formula "Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob" that recurs throughout the Hebrew Bible as shorthand for the patriarchal line (e.g., Exodus 3:6). Genesis's most-told story about him is not really his: Genesis 22, the binding of Isaac (the Akedah), where Abraham is commanded to sacrifice him and is stopped at the last moment — a story about Abraham's obedience in which Isaac himself is largely a passive figure. Compared to Abraham and Jacob, Isaac has little independent narrative in Genesis; most of his own chapters (24, 26) largely repeat plot beats already used for his father (a wife found through a servant/journey; a wife passed off as a sister to a foreign king).

Matthew's genealogy (1:2) uses Isaac purely as a link in the chain — "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob" — with no independent claim beyond the same patriarchal-narrative historicity question that applies to Abraham and Jacob generally: see Note 1. No extra-biblical source of any kind names Isaac or attests to any event in his specific story.

Cited in: Matthew 1:2; see Note 1.

ISAIAH

Isaiah ben Amoz, an 8th-century-BCE prophet active in Judah under kings Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, gives his name to the longest of the Latter Prophets. Matthew cites the book more than any other Old Testament source, treating "Isaiah" as a single continuous prophetic voice: the "voice of one crying in the wilderness" behind John the Baptist (Matthew 3:3, quoting Isaiah 40:3), the light dawning on Galilee (Matthew 4:14-16, quoting Isaiah 9:1-2), the servant who "took up our infirmities" (Matthew 8:17, quoting Isaiah 53:4), the servant who will not "break a bruised reed" (Matthew 12:17-21, quoting Isaiah 42:1-4), the parables that harden rather than reveal (Matthew 13:14-15, quoting Isaiah 6:9-10), and the people who honor God "with their lips" while their hearts are far away (Matthew 15:7-9, quoting Isaiah 29:13).

Since Bernhard Duhm's Das Buch Jesaia (Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 1892), part of the Handkommentar zum Alten Testament series, critical scholarship has treated the book as composite rather than the product of a single 8th-century author. Duhm split it into three blocks: chapters 1-39 ("Proto-Isaiah," attributable to Isaiah ben Amoz's own era), chapters 40-55 ("Deutero-Isaiah," an anonymous prophetic voice writing to the Babylonian exile community roughly a century and a half later), and chapters 56-66 ("Trito-Isaiah," a further, post-exilic layer).
