This three-part division remains the working framework of mainstream critical scholarship; Joseph Blenkinsopp's three-volume Anchor Bible commentary — Isaiah 1-39 (New York: Doubleday, 2000), Isaiah 40-55 (Doubleday, 2002), and Isaiah 56-66 (Doubleday, 2003) — treats each block as its own volume with its own historical setting, on this same premise.

Matthew's six citations draw from both halves of this scholarly division without distinction — three from Proto-Isaiah (4:14, 13:14, 15:7) and three from Deutero-Isaiah (3:3, 8:17, 12:17) — "Isaiah" functioning in the Gospel as a single unified prophetic authority regardless of which compositional layer, on the critical account, actually produced the words. The Deutero-Isaiah citations (8:17 and 12:17 in particular) draw on the Servant Songs, whose original audience and referent — collective Israel, a specific historical figure, or an idealized future figure — is a separate and long-running critical debate from the authorship question itself, one this entry flags rather than resolves.

Cited in: Matthew 3:3; 4:14; 8:17; 12:17; 13:14; 15:7.

ISRAEL / LAND OF ISRAEL

Matthew 2:20-21 has an angel tell Joseph to return "into the land of Israel," and Joseph does so. By this date there was no sovereign political state actually called "Israel" for Joseph to return to. The region was organized under Rome as a set of Herodian client territories — Judea, Samaria, and Idumea under Herod's son Archelaus as ethnarch (see JUDEA), Galilee and Perea under his son Antipas as tetrarch (see GALILEE) — not a unified kingdom bearing that name.

"Land of Israel" here is a scriptural-covenantal designation carried forward from the Hebrew Bible's own usage, where the phrase and its variants describe the territory promised to the patriarchs and settled by the twelve tribes, not a claim about contemporary Roman-era political geography. Matthew's Gospel uses it the way a modern writer might use "the Holy Land" — naming the land's scriptural identity rather than describing whichever administrative unit actually governed it at the time. The real governing entities Joseph was moving between were the Herodian tetrarchies and, within a few more years, direct Roman provincial rule over Judea (from 6 CE) — the gap between Matthew's terminology and the period's actual administrative map is a naming convention worth flagging for a modern reader, not a historical claim requiring its own independent verification.

Cited in: Matthew 2:20

ISRAEL-FIRST MISSION VS. GREAT COMMISSION (MATTHEW'S INTERNAL DEVELOPMENT)

The real, internal compositional tension between this chapter's restriction of the Twelve's mission to the lost sheep of the house of Israel alone, explicitly barring Gentiles and Samaritans (10:5-6), and this same Gospel's closing command to make disciples of all nations (28:19). Mainstream historical-critical scholarship reads the two passages as marking a genuine two-stage development in the early Jesus movement's own self-understanding — an Israel-focused mission during Jesus's ministry, expanding to a Gentile mission only after the resurrection — rather than treating the earlier restriction as an invented detail requiring harmonization away [189] [190].

JACOB, THE PATRIARCH

Isaac's son, grandson of Abraham, and — after wrestling a divine figure at the Jabbok ford (Genesis 32:22-32) — the man renamed Israel, whose twelve sons become the eponymous ancestors of the twelve tribes (Genesis 35:22-26). His Genesis narrative (chapters 25-50) is by far the longest and most developed of the three patriarchs': the deception of Esau for Isaac's blessing, fourteen years of labor for Laban to marry Rachel, the Joseph story that closes out the whole book. Matthew's genealogy compresses all of this to four words: "Isaac begat Jacob; and Jacob begat Judas and his brethren" (1:2).

This patriarchal Jacob must not be confused with the other Jacob named later in the very same genealogy: "Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary" (1:16) — Joseph's father, a completely different man living roughly eighteen centuries (by the text's own internal chronology) after the patriarch. Matthew's genealogy uses the name twice for two unrelated individuals separated by dozens of generations, which is easy to misread as a single figure spanning the whole family tree; it is not — Genesis's Jacob-Israel and Joseph's father Jacob (Matthew 1:16) are two distinct people who share only a name.

The historicity question for the patriarchal Jacob is the same one covered for Abraham and Isaac: see Note 1 for the Albright/Kitchen traditionalist position against Thompson, Van Seters, and Redford's critical position that the patriarchal narratives reflect a later composition rather than a preserved Bronze Age family history.

Cited in: Matthew 1:2 (the patriarch); distinguish Matthew 1:16 (Joseph's father, a different Jacob); see Note 1.

JAMES, BROTHER OF JESUS

Listed first among Jesus's four named brothers at Matthew 13:55 ("James, and Joseph, and Simon, and Judas" — see JOSEPH, BROTHER OF JESUS; SIMON, BROTHER OF JESUS; JUDAS, BROTHER OF JESUS). Outside the Gospels, James is independently attested by Josephus (Jewish Antiquities 20.9.1), who records that the high priest Ananus had "the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James" brought before the Sanhedrin and stoned to death, around 62 CE — one of the clearer non-Christian corroborations of a named New Testament figure's existence and fate, earlier than and independent of the fuller, more legendary account of James's death given by the 2nd-century Christian writer Hegesippus (preserved only in Eusebius). Paul's letters independently confirm a James active in the Jerusalem church, calling him "the Lord's brother" (Galatians 1:19) and giving him a leadership role there (Galatians 2:9; Acts 15).

A limestone ossuary surfacing on the antiquities market in 2002, bearing an Aramaic inscription commonly translated "James, son of Joseph, brother of Jesus," was announced by biblical scholar André Lemaire in Biblical Archaeology Review ("Burial Box of James the Brother of Jesus," Nov/Dec 2002, pp. 24-33, 70) as a possible first physical link to this specific New Testament family. The Israel Antiquities Authority concluded in 2003 that the "brother of Jesus" portion of the inscription was a modern forgery added to an otherwise genuine ancient box, and the ossuary's owner, Israeli collector Oded Golan, was charged in 2004 with running a forgery operation. A seven-year trial — reportedly running to 138 witnesses and over 12,000 pages of testimony — ended in Golan's 2012 acquittal on the forgery charges; the presiding judge's ruling cleared Golan criminally but did not affirmatively certify the inscription as genuine evidence of this James, leaving the ossuary's evidentiary value genuinely contested rather than resolved in either direction.

Cited in: Matthew 13:55; see JOSEPH, BROTHER OF JESUS; SIMON, BROTHER OF JESUS; JUDAS, BROTHER OF JESUS.

JAMES, SON OF ALPHAEUS

Named identically in all four apostle lists (Matthew 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:15; Acts 1:13) by his patronymic alone, with no further action or speech attributed to him anywhere in the New Testament — one of the most anonymous of the Twelve even by that group's sparse standard. He is often popularly identified with "James the less" (or "the younger" — Greek *ho mikros*, Mark 15:40), whose mother is named "Mary" in the same verse and who may in turn be the "Mary, wife of Clopas" named at the crucifixion (John 19:25) — "Clopas" and "Alphaeus" being plausibly, though not certainly, the same underlying name rendered two different ways in Greek. None of these identifications is stated outright by any text; each rests on matching partial details across separate passages, the same kind of inferential chain used to link Thaddaeus with Judas son of James (see THADDAEUS) and Bartholomew with Nathanael (see BARTHOLOMEW).

If Mark 2:14's naming of Levi as "son of Alphaeus" is taken at face value, it additionally raises whether this James and Matthew/Levi were brothers (see MATTHEW (LEVI)) — a real possibility the text never confirms.

Cited in: Matthew 10:3; see MATTHEW (LEVI).

JAMES, SON OF ZEBEDEE

One of Zebedee's two fisherman sons (see ZEBEDEE), called from the boat alongside his brother John (Matthew 4:21-22). Jesus gives the brothers the nickname "Boanerges," rendered "sons of thunder" (Mark 3:17) — though the underlying Aramaic this transliterates is genuinely unsettled even among specialists: proposed readings include "sons of rage/tumult" rather than a word actually meaning thunder, and the Aramaic scholar Maurice Casey has argued the whole form may simply be a scribal misreading of the Aramaic word for thunder (this entry has not independently verified which specific Casey publication makes the argument, only that the position is attributed to him in the secondary literature). The nickname is real; its precise derivation is not fully settled.

James is, uniquely among the Twelve, the one apostle whose death the New Testament itself records: Acts 12:2 states that Herod Agrippa I had him executed by the sword, conventionally dated around 44 CE — the single best-attested apostolic death by scripture's own account, independent of any later legend.

The tradition that his body was later carried to Compostela, in Spain, and that he evangelized Spain in his lifetime, is a medieval legend with no source earlier than several centuries after the fact. It surfaces alongside, and serves the interests of, the Reconquista-era Iberian church — a clear case of legendary accretion layered onto a figure whose actual death is otherwise unusually well-documented for an apostle.

Cited in: Matthew 4:21; see JOHN SON OF ZEBEDEE, ZEBEDEE.

JEREMIAH

Jeremiah ben Hilkiah, a prophet active in Judah from the reign of Josiah through the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem in 587/586 BCE, is invoked by name three times in Matthew. At 2:17-18 he is cited for "Rachel weeping for her children" (Jeremiah 31:15), applied to Herod's slaughter of the infants at Bethlehem. At 16:14, when Jesus asks the disciples who people say he is, "Jeremiah" is offered as one of the guesses alongside Elijah and the prophets generally — reflecting some strand of expectation that Jeremiah himself might return. At 27:9-10, Matthew again names Jeremiah as the source of a prophecy fulfilled in Judas's thirty pieces of silver and the potter's field.

The 27:9 citation is a genuine, long-discussed textual problem rather than a settled point. The wording Matthew quotes — thirty pieces of silver, thrown into the house of the LORD, the price of "him that was valued," given for a potter — tracks Zechariah 11:12-13 far more closely than anything in the book of Jeremiah, even though Jeremiah does contain adjacent imagery (a potter's house in 18:1-11, a purchased field in 32:6-9, and a smashed pot at the potter's-field site of Topheth in 19:1-13) that Matthew appears to be folding in alongside the Zechariah wording. Commentators have proposed several explanations without full consensus: that Matthew is deliberately blending two prophetic passages and names only the more prominent of the two (a documented ancient practice — Mark 1:2-3 does something structurally similar, naming only Isaiah while quoting both Isaiah and Malachi); that an early scribal error substituted one prophet's name for the other; or that Matthew had a specific, non-canonical "Jeremiah" tradition in view. See R.T. France, The Gospel of Matthew (New International Commentary on the New Testament; Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 2007), and D.A. Carson, "Matthew," in The Expositor's Bible Commentary, vol. 8 (Grand Rapids: Zondervan, 1984), both of which treat the citation as a composite drawing primarily on Zechariah's wording under Jeremiah's name (page references not verified).

Cited in: Matthew 2:17; 16:14; 27:9.

JERICHO

One of the oldest continuously-inhabited sites in the world, on the west bank of the Jordan River near the Dead Sea. Appears in Matthew 20:29, Mark 10:46, and Luke 18:35 as a stop on Jesus's route to Jerusalem (the healing of Bartimaeus, and, in Luke, Zacchaeus the tax collector). Its older and far more famous scriptural role is Joshua 6: the city whose walls "came tumbling down" after the Israelites marched around it seven times — the founding legend of the conquest narrative.

Kathleen Kenyon's 1952-1958 excavation at Tell es-Sultan (the site's ancient tell), using her own Wheeler-Kenyon stratigraphic method, dated the relevant destruction layer to roughly 1550 BCE — the end of the Middle Bronze Age. This is centuries earlier than the traditional biblical conquest date of roughly 1400 BCE that an earlier excavator, John Garstang, had argued the site's evidence supported. Kenyon's redating (based mainly on the absence of a specific imported Cypriot pottery type used as a dating marker) has stuck as the widely accepted conclusion and became a foundational piece of evidence for later critical/minimalist readings of the conquest narrative generally.

For the Gospel-era mentions (Matthew 20:29, Mark 10:46, Luke 18:35), none of this is in dispute: Jericho's existence and location as a real, inhabited 1st-century city on the Jerusalem road are not contested — a live, identifiable place matching known Roman-period geography, entirely separate from the earlier Bronze Age dating controversy attached to the Joshua conquest story.

Cited in: 3 (Kathleen Kenyon's excavation, indirectly, via the broader conquest-historicity question this entry flags for future chapters); full Gospel-ministry treatment pending as the book reaches Matthew 20/Mark 10/Luke 18.

JERUSALEM

City in the Judean hill country, continuously inhabited for at least three millennia and one of the most heavily excavated urban sites on earth. By the time Matthew's narrative reaches it, Jerusalem is the provincial center of Roman Judaea, seat of Herodian and (during the Passion) direct Roman prefectural authority, and home to the Second Temple (see THE TEMPLE). Matthew's Gospel first names the city at 2:1, when magi arrive asking after "the King of the Jews" — a mention that ties Jerusalem to political anxiety (Herod's, 2:3) before Jesus ever enters it in the narrative; the city becomes the fixed destination of the whole Passion sequence from 21:1 onward.

Unlike most of the individual sites and episodes this Glossary treats one by one, Jerusalem's own existence, location, and status as Judaea's capital in the early 1st century CE are not in scholarly dispute of any kind. Continuous excavation since the 19th century — most extensively Dame Kathleen Kenyon's 1961-1967 campaigns on the City of David's southeastern hill and around the Old City walls — has mapped the city's urban boundaries, water systems, and building phases across periods in a level of documented detail matched by few other places named anywhere in the New Testament. The genuinely open questions this book returns to again and again are not "did Jerusalem exist" but which specific spot within it corresponds to a given Gospel scene — where the Temple's inner courts actually stood, where Pilate held court, where the crucifixion and burial took place. Each of those has its own entry below (see THE TEMPLE; PRAETORIUM; GOLGOTHA).

Cited in: Matthew 2:1; recurs throughout the Passion-week chapters (21-28).

JESUS (CHRIST)

Introduced in Matthew 1:1 as "Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham," the subject of the whole book carries several distinct titles across the text, each with its own history rather than being interchangeable synonyms. "Christ" (Greek christos, "anointed one") translates the Hebrew mashiach and was originally a functional title - applied in the Hebrew Bible to kings and priests literally anointed with oil - not a proper name and not, by default, a single agreed-upon end-times figure. "Son of God" and "Son of Man" both appear as titles applied to Jesus; "Son of Man" is in fact the term the Synoptic Gospels most often place in Jesus's own mouth as self-reference, and its exact force (a plain Aramaic idiom for "a person," an allusion to the enthroned figure of Daniel 7:13-14, or both at once) remains debated among scholars. Matthew alone glosses "Emmanuel" (1:23, quoting Isaiah 7:14) as "God with us" for a Greek-reading audience unfamiliar with the Hebrew. "Rabbi" or "Teacher" (used by disciples and outsiders alike) and "Lord" (kyrios, the same Greek word the Septuagint uses to render God's own name) round out the set of titles actually used on the page.

Mainstream historical-critical scholarship - represented by, among others, E. P. Sanders's The Historical Figure of Jesus (Penguin Books, 1993) and John P. Meier's multi-volume A Marginal Jew: Rethinking the Historical Jesus (Vol. 1, Doubleday, 1991, Anchor Bible Reference Library) - holds that a real, itinerant first-century Jewish teacher and prophet named Jesus of Nazareth existed, was baptized by John the Baptist (see JOHN THE BAPTIST), gathered followers, and was executed under the Roman prefect Pontius Pilate; this bare historical core is treated as close to as settled as any claim of comparable age in ancient history gets. Whether he was the Messiah, the Son of God in a metaphysical sense, or divine are theological claims this project's method does not adjudicate - they are questions of faith, not questions the surviving evidentiary record can settle in either direction, and this entry does not attempt to.

Cited in: Matthew 1:1; see JOHN THE BAPTIST.

JOHN THE BAPTIST

Introduced at Matthew 3:1 as a wilderness preacher active in Jesus's early adulthood, baptizing crowds in the Jordan and warning of coming judgment; Matthew 14:1-12 later narrates his imprisonment and beheading by Herod Antipas, prompted — in Matthew's telling — by John's public objection to Antipas's marriage to Herodias, his brother's wife, with Herodias's daughter's dance at a banquet securing his execution as a reward from the king.

John is one of the few Gospel figures independently corroborated by a non-Christian contemporary source. Josephus, writing decades later in Jewish Antiquities 18.5.2, confirms a real preacher called "the Baptist" who "commanded the Jews to lead righteous lives" and was executed by Herod Antipas at the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea. This is a genuine independent cross-check on both a Gospel figure's existence and the bare fact of his manner of death — but Josephus gives an entirely different stated motive than the Gospels do. In Josephus's account, Antipas feared John's popular influence over the crowds might let him "raise a rebellion," and had him killed as a preemptive political measure; there is no mention anywhere in Josephus of Herodias, a daughter, a dance, or a birthday banquet. The two sources do not contradict each other on the bare fact of John's execution by Antipas at Machaerus — they diverge entirely on why, offering two independently plausible motives (a political threat and a personal grudge) that are not strictly mutually exclusive but were never reconciled by either source.

This entry has not independently verified a specific modern critical edition/translation of Josephus and cites him, following this project's nativity-chronology convention, by his standard internal reference numbers only.

Cited in: Matthew 3:1, 14:1-12.

JOHN, SON OF ZEBEDEE

The younger of Zebedee's two fisherman sons (see ZEBEDEE), called alongside his brother James (Matthew 4:21-22) and given the same "Boanerges"/"sons of thunder" nickname (Mark 3:17; see JAMES, SON OF ZEBEDEE).

Tradition conflates John son of Zebedee with several figures who may or may not be the same person: "John the Evangelist" (the traditional author of the Fourth Gospel), "John the Elder" (named separately by the early-2nd-century bishop Papias), and "John of Patmos" (author of Revelation). None of the Gospels ever name John son of Zebedee as their author, and the Fourth Gospel's famous reference to "the disciple whom Jesus loved" (John 13:23, 19:26, 21:20) never states that this figure is John son of Zebedee at all — the identification is a longstanding, widespread traditional inference, not something the text itself asserts.

The tradition placing his tomb at Ephesus is attested no earlier than the 2nd century, via Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus, as later quoted by the church historian Eusebius in his *Ecclesiastical History* (4th century) — meaning even this relatively strong tradition postdates any living memory of the man himself by generations.

Cited in: Matthew 4:21; see JAMES SON OF ZEBEDEE, ZEBEDEE.

JONAH

Jonah ben Amittai appears in Matthew only as a rhetorical sign: "an evil and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign; and there shall no sign be given to it, but the sign of the prophet Jonah" (Matthew 12:39, repeated at 16:4), with 12:40 explicitly comparing Jonah's three days and nights "in the whale's belly" to Jesus's coming three days in the tomb, and 12:41 holding up "the men of Nineveh" who repented at Jonah's preaching as a standing judgment against the current generation.

The book of Jonah is widely treated by critical scholars as a distinct genre from the historical narrative and oracular collections that make up the rest of the Twelve (Minor) Prophets — closer to satire, parable, or (in Jack M. Sasson's phrase) a "didactic, satiric novella" than to reportage. Jack M. Sasson, Jonah: A New Translation with Introduction, Commentary, and Interpretations (Anchor Bible 24B; New York: Doubleday, 1990), surveys the major source-critical and genre debates and is the standard critical commentary on the book. Details commonly cited in favor of a non-historical reading include the story's exaggerated scale (Nineveh described in Jonah 3:3 as a three-day walk across, and its king — unnamed and otherwise unattested — issuing a repentance decree that extends even to the city's livestock, Jonah 3:7-8) and the book's satirical treatment of its own prophet, who sulks at God's mercy rather than celebrating it.

Nineveh's actual destruction is independently and solidly attested: it fell to a combined Median-Babylonian assault in 612 BCE, an event recorded in the so-called Chronicle of Nabopolassar (British Museum tablet BM 21901), first published in C.J. Gadd, The Fall of Nineveh: The Newly-Discovered Babylonian Chronicle No. 21,901 in the British Museum (London: Harrison and Sons, 1923). That contemporary Babylonian record — written from the winning side, with no interest in the biblical narrative — corroborates that Nineveh was a real city that met a real, datable end; it says nothing about the specific repentance episode the book of Jonah describes roughly a century and a half earlier, in the reign attributed to the historical Jonah's presumed contemporary, Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:25), and offers no way to adjudicate that separate, disputed episode.

Cited in: Matthew 12:39-41; 16:4.

JORDAN RIVER

A real, geographically uncontroversial river — the setting of John's baptizing ministry (Matthew 3:6) and of Jesus's own baptism (Matthew 3:13–17). The river's existence, course, and identity are not disputed by any position on the spectrum.

What is disputed is the exact spot. Two modern sites compete for the title of "the" baptism location, on opposite banks: Qasr al-Yahud, on the West Bank side across from Jericho, and Al-Maghtas (also called Bethany-Beyond-the-Jordan), on the Jordanian east bank about nine kilometers north of the Dead Sea. Excavations at Al-Maghtas since 1997 have uncovered Byzantine- and Roman-period churches, a monastery, hermit caves, and baptismal pools, and UNESCO added the site to its World Heritage List in 2015 under the name "Baptism Site 'Bethany Beyond the Jordan' (Al-Maghtas)," citing continuous Christian veneration there from at least the late Roman/early Byzantine period onward. Qasr al-Yahud, closed for decades due to its location in a militarized zone, reopened to visitors in 2011 and draws its own pilgrim traffic.

Both sites have genuine, physically excavated evidence of centuries of Christian pilgrimage and commemorative building activity going back to the Byzantine era — but neither has, or could have, direct archaeological proof of being the literal spot of a first-century event with no contemporary marker. The tradition is old and real; the precise identification is inherited devotion, not verified geography.

Cited in: Matthew (beat covering 3:6, 3:13).

JOSEPH (JOSES), BROTHER OF JESUS

The second of Jesus's four brothers named at Matthew 13:55; Mark's parallel list (6:3) gives the same name in its shorter Greek form, "Joses" — a common period diminutive of Joseph, not a different name for a different person. Sharing a name with his father (see JOSEPH, HUSBAND OF MARY) reflects the genuinely narrow pool of common male names in this period and place: Tal Ilan's Lexicon of Jewish Names in Late Antiquity, Part I: Palestine 330 BCE-200 CE (Mohr Siebeck, 2002) catalogues Simon, Joseph, and Judah as the three most frequently attested Jewish male names on record for the era, from a combination of literary, epigraphic, and papyrological sources — three of Jesus's own four named brothers carry exactly these three names.

No independent source outside the Gospels mentions this Joseph, and nothing further is said of him anywhere in the New Testament: no teaching attributed to him, no later leadership role in the Jerusalem church of the kind Acts and Paul's letters give his brother James (see JAMES, BROTHER OF JESUS), no later tradition of martyrdom or authorship attached to his name the way tradition attaches an epistle to his brother Judas (see JUDAS, BROTHER OF JESUS). On the surviving record, he is a name only.

Cited in: Matthew 13:55, Mark 6:3; see JAMES, BROTHER OF JESUS; JOSEPH, HUSBAND OF MARY.

JOSEPH OF ARIMATHEA

Introduced at Matthew 27:57-60 as "a rich man... named Joseph," a disciple of Jesus who requests Jesus's body from Pilate after the crucifixion and buries it in his own new, unused rock-cut tomb. Mark (15:43), Luke (23:50-51), and John (19:38) each add detail Matthew omits or leaves implicit: Mark and Luke both call him a member of the Sanhedrin (Luke adding that he had not consented to that council's condemnation of Jesus), and John describes him as a disciple who kept his allegiance secret "for fear of the Jews." He is one of several men named Joseph across the Gospels and Acts — distinct from Joseph the husband of Mary, from Jesus's brother Joseph/Joses, and from Joseph Barsabbas, a candidate to replace Judas Iscariot in Acts 1:23 (a name so common that, per Tal Ilan's Lexicon of Jewish Names, it ranks among the three most frequently attested Jewish male names of the period — see JOSEPH (JOSES), BROTHER OF JESUS).

The town of Arimathea itself has no confirmed independent attestation outside the Gospels and cannot be located with certainty on the ground. The 4th-century historian Eusebius of Caesarea identified it with Ramathaim-Zophim, the hometown of the prophet Samuel (1 Samuel 1:1), near Diospolis (modern Lod) — a plausible but unconfirmed identification resting on a similar name rather than independent geographic or archaeological evidence. No inscription, administrative record, or non-Christian source of any kind confirms a first-century town by this name.

Cited in: Matthew 27:57-60; see JOSEPH, HUSBAND OF MARY; JOSEPH (JOSES), BROTHER OF JESUS.

JOSEPH, HUSBAND OF MARY

Named in Matthew 1:16 as the husband of Mary and, through Matthew's genealogy (1:1-16), the legal line connecting Jesus to King David — see this project's genealogies-of-jesus grounding document for how that lineage is constructed, and where it conflicts with Luke's. Matthew 13:55 gives his trade as tekton, conventionally rendered "carpenter" but covering a wider range of manual building work in Koine Greek — mason and general craftsman are equally defensible translations, and nothing in the surviving record narrows it further.

Joseph receives angelic instruction three separate times in Matthew's infancy narrative alone (1:20-21, 2:13, 2:19-20) and acts on each one immediately and without recorded objection or spoken reply — a repeated narrative pattern, not an incidental detail, and one that leaves Joseph as a Gospel figure who never has a recorded line of his own dialogue anywhere in the New Testament. After the family's return from Egypt and resettlement in Nazareth (2:19-23), he is never mentioned again by name in Matthew's text.

Most scholars infer Joseph died sometime before Jesus's adult ministry began, on the strength of his total absence from every Gospel's account of that ministry and moments such as John 19:26-27, where Jesus's mother appears with no corresponding mention of a living husband. This is a reasonable inference from silence, not a fact the New Testament states outright anywhere.

Cited in: Matthew 1:16, 13:55; see MARY, MOTHER OF JESUS.

JUDAS ISCARIOT

Named last in all three Synoptic lists, always with a note of what he would do (Matthew 10:4: "who also betrayed him"; similarly Mark 3:19, Luke 6:16). John's Gospel gives him a patronymic, "son of Simon Iscariot" (John 6:71, 13:26) — the only apostle given a named father other than the two sets of brothers who already carry one (Zebedee's sons, Alphaeus's son). "Iscariot" is most widely read, following the 4th-5th century church father Jerome, as a Hellenized form of Hebrew *ish-Kerioth*, "man of Kerioth" — Kerioth being a real town named in Joshua 15:25 (in Judea) and again, possibly a different place of the same name, in Amos 2:2 (in Moab; see MOAB). A minority alternative etymology ties it instead to the Latin *sicarius*, "dagger-man," the term for the Sicarii, a cadre of Jewish assassins active against Rome — but most historians reject this reading as anachronistic, since the Sicarii are not attested as an organized group until the 40s-50s CE, too late to plausibly name a man executed years earlier.

Beyond the betrayal narrative, the New Testament gives two accounts of his death that do not describe the same event and are never reconciled by either author: Matthew 27:3-10 has him hang himself after returning the thirty pieces of silver, while Acts 1:18 has him fall headlong in a field purchased with that same money and burst open. No harmonization is attempted by either text — the single clearest internal contradiction attached to any member of the Twelve.

Cited in: Matthew 10:4, 26:14-16, 27:3-10; see THADDAEUS.

JUDAS, BROTHER OF JESUS

The last of Jesus's four named brothers at Matthew 13:55 — not to be confused with Judas Iscariot, the betrayer, or Judas (also called Thaddaeus) the apostle (Matthew 10:3). Christian tradition since antiquity has identified this Judas with the author of the New Testament's short Epistle of Jude, whose opening verse identifies its writer as "Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James" (Jude 1:1) — a self-description read, since the letter names no other identifying detail, as most plausibly pointing back to this same brother of Jesus and James (see JAMES, BROTHER OF JESUS), on the assumption that "brother of James" invokes the same James who led the Jerusalem church.

This identification is not certain. Modern critical scholarship widely treats the Epistle of Jude as a pseudonymous composition from the late first or early second century, written under this Judas's name and authority rather than by his own hand — a common and well-attested practice in the period for letters circulated under an authoritative figure's name — and some scholars question whether "brother" in the letter's own self-description was even meant literally (a family relationship) rather than as a term for close spiritual kinship. No independent, non-Christian source mentions this Judas at all.

Cited in: Matthew 13:55; see JAMES, BROTHER OF JESUS.

JUDEA

The southern portion of the region, containing Jerusalem, and the seat of Herod the Great's kingdom (Matt 2:1). Judea's political status changes across the span Matthew's narrative covers, tracking three distinct rulers the text itself names. Herod the Great governed as a Roman client king until his death, dated by Josephus (Jewish Antiquities 17.6.4, 17.9.3) to shortly before Passover, c. 4 BCE (see the nativity chronology). His will, largely ratified by Augustus, split the kingdom among his surviving sons: Archelaus received Judea, Samaria, and Idumea, but only with the lesser title ethnarch, not king (Matt 2:22 names him directly). Archelaus's rule proved unpopular enough that Rome deposed him in 6 CE and annexed Judea as a directly administered Roman territory governed by prefects, the first being Coponius (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 18.1.1); Pontius Pilate, the best-attested of these prefects, served from 26 to 36 CE.

This progression — client king, to client ethnarch, to direct Roman provincial rule — is independently well documented (E. Mary Smallwood, The Jews Under Roman Rule: From Pompey to Diocletian, Brill, 1976; Fergus Millar, The Roman Near East, 31 BC-AD 337, Harvard University Press, 1993) and is not itself in dispute. The genuinely debated questions attached to Judea in this period belong to specific episodes — the Herod/Quirinius census gap, Pilate's own tenure and character (see PONTIUS PILATE) — not to the basic administrative facts of who governed the territory when.

Cited in: Matthew 2:1

KADDISH AND AMIDAH (JEWISH LITURGICAL PARALLELS)

Two closely related first-century Jewish liturgical forms whose petitions the Lord's Prayer (6:9-13) recognizably compresses: the Kaddish, an Aramaic prayer sanctifying God's name and petitioning for God's kingdom that concluded the synagogue service, and the Amidah (the Eighteen Benedictions), Second Temple Judaism's standing prayer of fixed daily petitions for sustenance, forgiveness, and deliverance. Joachim Jeremias's classic study first drew the comparison in detail; later critical commentary finds the parallel holds petition by petition, not just thematically, with the Amidah's ninth benediction occupying roughly the same structural position as the Lord's Prayer's bread petition [125] [126] [128]. The Amidah's fixed, numbered form is somewhat later than Jesus's own lifetime, codified at Yavneh after 70 CE, though specific constituent petitions are argued to predate the Temple's destruction [127]. None of this makes the Lord's Prayer's content less original to Jesus; it situates it as a distinctively Christian condensation of recognizably Jewish prayer forms, not an unprecedented new genre.

KEYS OF THE KINGDOM (ISAIAH 22:22 BACKGROUND)

Jesus's grant to Peter, "I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 16:19), paired with the power to "bind" and "loose" on earth and in heaven. The image is not invented for this scene: it draws on Isaiah 22:15-22, where the prophet Eliakim son of Hilkiah, Judah's royal steward, is given "the key of the house of David" on his shoulder, with authority to open what no one can shut and shut what no one can open — a genuine ancient Near Eastern image of a king's chief household officer holding delegated administrative authority [252]. Like the rock-naming beside it, this material appears only in Matthew's telling of the Caesarea Philippi scene, with no parallel in Mark or Luke [251].

LORD'S PRAYER (TEXTUAL HISTORY)

The prayer Jesus teaches his disciples at 6:9-13, whose transmission history contains two well-documented, checkable puzzles distinct from the prayer's content itself. First, the familiar closing doxology ('for thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever, Amen') is absent from the earliest and best Greek manuscripts and from Luke's parallel version entirely, and is judged by the near-universal consensus of textual critics to be a later liturgical addition rather than part of Matthew's original text [129] [130]; the Didache already attests an early but differently-worded doxology by the early second century [131]. Second, the familiar English 'forgive us our trespasses' rests on a conflation: Matthew's actual Greek word at 6:12 is opheilemata, a financial-debt term, while 'trespasses' derives from paraptomata, the different word Matthew uses two verses later at 6:14-15 [132], a substitution traceable to William Tyndale's 1526 translation choice [133].

MACHAERUS (FORTRESS)

A Herodian hilltop fortress east of the Dead Sea, in modern Jordan, identified by the first-century historian Flavius Josephus as the prison where Herod Antipas held John the Baptist and where John was executed (Jewish Antiquities 18.5.2) — a location Matthew's own account of John's imprisonment (11:2) never names (see JOHN THE BAPTIST for the fuller Josephus comparison, including where his account diverges from the Gospels on John's motive). The site is not a matter of later pilgrimage guesswork: since 2009 a Hungarian Academy of Arts mission led by Gyozo Voros, working under the Studium Biblicum Franciscanum in Jerusalem, has excavated and reconstructed the fortress across multiple campaigns, publishing full findings in the three-volume Machaerus series (Collectio Maior 53, 55, 56; 2013-2019), confirming a fortified Herodian royal palace-citadel matching Josephus's description on the ground [199].

Cited in: Matthew (beat covering 11:1-2).

MAGADAN

The place Matthew 15:39 names as the destination of Jesus's boat after the feeding of the four thousand — except the parallel account of the identical episode, ending at the identical narrative beat (Pharisees immediately demanding a sign), names a different place: Mark 8:10 has "Dalmanutha" instead of "Magadan." This is a genuine, unresolved textual and geographic crux, not a simple spelling variant.

Neither name is independently attested anywhere outside these two verses — no mention in Josephus, no inscription, no other Gospel, no external geographic source of any kind for either "Magadan" or "Dalmanutha." The leading scholarly theory holds that "Magadan" is a corrupted or variant form of "Magdala" (home village of Mary Magdalene per Luke 8:2), a real fishing town on the lake's western shore whose remains near modern Migdal are independently identified with Josephus's Taricheae — with Hebrew/Aramaic "l" and "n" sometimes interchanging in transmission. "Dalmanutha" has no comparable candidate at all and remains completely unlocated.

Some manuscripts of Matthew read "Magdala" directly rather than "Magadan," which, if original, would resolve the crux cleanly — but the earliest and best-attested manuscripts favor the otherwise-unknown "Magadan," leaving the location of this episode formally unidentified in both Gospels.

Cited in: Matthew (beat covering 15:39).

MALACHI (PROPHET)

The prophetic book (traditionally dated to the fifth century BCE, in the early post-exilic Persian period) that closes the Hebrew Bible's Twelve Minor Prophets and, in its final verses, promises that God will send 'the prophet Elijah before the great and terrible day of the LORD comes' to turn the hearts of parents and children toward each other (Malachi 4:5-6; numbered 3:23-24 in the Hebrew Bible/Jewish Publication Society tradition) [201]. This specific promise is the scriptural basis for Jesus's direct identification of John the Baptist with the returning Elijah at Matthew 11:14 (see ELIJAH for the fuller history of that identification across the four Gospels, including the Fourth Gospel's contrary account of John denying the title himself).

Cited in: Matthew (beat covering 11:2-15).

MARY MAGDALENE

Named at Matthew 27:56, 27:61, and 28:1 among the women present at the crucifixion, the burial, and the empty tomb — one of the most consistently attested figures across all four Gospels at exactly the moments that matter most to the Passion and resurrection narratives. "Magdalene" most likely designates her hometown, Magdala, a fishing town on the Sea of Galilee, rather than a family or married name; nothing in Matthew, Mark, Luke, or John describes her as a "sinner," a prostitute, or connects her to any anointing scene.

That association is a documented later addition to her story, not a scriptural claim at all. In 591, Pope Gregory I, in a homily on the Gospels delivered on one of the year's September Ember days (a quarterly fast, not Easter) and preserved as Homily 33 of his Homiliae in Evangelia, publicly merged three separate New Testament women — Mary Magdalene, Mary of Bethany, and the unnamed "sinful woman" who anoints Jesus's feet in Luke 7:36-50 — into a single composite figure, reasoning that the "seven demons" Luke 8:2 says were cast out of Mary Magdalene represented the seven deadly sins, including lust. As Susan Haskins documents in Mary Magdalene: Myth and Metaphor (HarperCollins, 1993), this one sermon fixed Mary Magdalene's popular image as a repentant prostitute in Western Christianity for close to fourteen centuries, despite having no basis in the Gospel text itself; the Catholic Church's own liturgical calendar reform under Pope Paul VI in 1969 formally separated the three women again, restoring Mary Magdalene's own, distinct Gospel identity.

Cited in: Matthew 27:56, 27:61, 28:1.

MARY, MOTHER OF JAMES AND JOSEPH ("THE OTHER MARY")

Named at Matthew 27:56 as one of the women watching the crucifixion "afar off," identified there as "Mary the mother of James and Joses" (using the same short form of "Joseph" discussed at JOSEPH (JOSES), BROTHER OF JESUS — a separate man of the same name, not to be confused with him). Matthew 27:61 and 28:1 then refer to her simply as "the other Mary," distinguishing her from Mary Magdalene without repeating her fuller description each time.

Many scholars identify this woman with "Mary the wife of Clopas," named at the cross in John's independent account (John 19:25) as a relative of Jesus's mother — a comparison across Gospel witness-lists that Anglican scholar Stephen S. Smalley, writing in 1982, judged "probable." If correct, this would make her the aunt of Jesus by marriage. The identification is not certain: it depends on further equating "Clopas" with "Cleopas," the disciple named on the road to Emmaus in Luke 24:18, and further still with "Alphaeus," father of the apostle James (Matthew 10:3) — a chain of three separate name-equations, each individually plausible, none independently confirmed, and complicated by the fact that Luke's own Gospel uses both "Cleophas" and "Alphaeus" without ever treating them as the same name.

Cited in: Matthew 27:56, 27:61, 28:1; see JOSEPH (JOSES), BROTHER OF JESUS.

MARY, MOTHER OF JESUS

Named at Matthew 1:16, 1:18-25, and 2:11 as Joseph's betrothed and then wife, and the mother whose pregnancy "of the Holy Spirit" (1:18) Matthew frames as fulfilling Isaiah 7:14 — the virginal-conception claim, and the Hebrew almah/Greek parthenos translation question underlying it, examined in full in this project's nativity-chronology grounding document. Matthew's infancy narrative is told almost entirely from Joseph's point of view; Luke's parallel account, by contrast, centers Mary's own experience (the angel's direct address to her, her own song at 1:46-55), and Matthew gives Mary no recorded speech of her own at all.

"Mary" (Miriam in Hebrew) was among the most common women's names in first-century Judea, and the Gospels name several distinct women who share it — a real identification hazard the text never resolves for the reader on its own. Matthew 27:56 names three at once: Mary Magdalene, "Mary the mother of James and Joseph," and — read alongside John 19:25, since Matthew does not repeat "mother of Jesus" at the cross the way John does — very likely a third distinct Mary as well. This entry covers Jesus's own mother specifically.

Cited in: Matthew 1:16, 1:18-25, 2:11; see JOSEPH, HUSBAND OF MARY; MARY MAGDALENE; MARY, MOTHER OF JAMES AND JOSEPH.

MASHAL (RABBINIC PARABLE FORM)

The short, realistic or semi-realistic Jewish narrative form, typically paired with an explicit application, preserved by the hundreds in later classical Midrash and the Talmud and cited in this chapter as the attested genre Jesus's parable-teaching most closely resembles [217]. Rabbinic meshalim routinely assign meaning to several narrative details at once rather than making one isolated point, a feature scholars argue is directly relevant to reading the sower's own multi-part explanation (13:18-23) [218].

MASSACRE OF THE INNOCENTS (HISTORICITY QUESTION)

Herod's order, per Matthew alone, to kill every boy two years old or under in and around Bethlehem after the Magi fail to report back to him (2:16-18). No source outside Matthew records the event, including Josephus, whose extensive, unfriendly catalogue of Herod's real cruelties never mentions it [72]; a fifth-century joke attributed to Augustus is sometimes cited as external confirmation but is too late and too derivative to serve as independent evidence [71]. The minority argument for historicity rests on Bethlehem's small, disputed population [73]; the majority historical-critical reading treats the episode as a theological composition modeled on Pharaoh's decree against Hebrew infants in Exodus 1-2 [74].

MATAN BA-SETER (ANONYMOUS CHARITY)

The Hebrew term for 'giving in secret,' the developed halakhic concept most famously systematized by Maimonides in his twelfth-century eight-rung ladder of charity, which ranks anonymous giving to an unknown recipient near its highest tiers [136]. The underlying value is considerably older than Maimonides's system: the Jerusalem Temple maintained an actual 'Chamber of Secrets' where donations and support changed hands anonymously [135], the Babylonian Talmud credits Rabbi Elazar with ranking secret charity above Moses [137], and the ethic traces back further still into Second Temple-period wisdom literature such as the book of Tobit [138]. Jesus's instruction that the left hand not know what the right hand is doing (6:3) assumes this already-established Jewish value rather than introducing a new one.

MATTHEW (LEVI)

A tax collector (Greek *telones*) called from his tax booth (Matthew 9:9) — one of the more socially loaded callings among the Twelve, since tax collectors in Roman Judea worked within a system widely resented for extortion and collaboration with Rome. Matthew's own Gospel names him "Matthew" at the calling; the parallel accounts of the same event in Mark 2:14 and Luke 5:27 both name the man called "Levi," and Mark additionally identifies him as "Levi son of Alphaeus." No text explicitly states that Matthew and Levi are the same person — it is a traditional harmonization built from reading the three call narratives as one event, not something any single Gospel asserts directly.

If the Mark 2:14 patronymic is accepted, it raises an unresolved question: another apostle, James, is separately named "son of Alphaeus" in all four lists (Matthew 10:3; see JAMES SON OF ALPHAEUS). Whether this means Matthew/Levi and James son of Alphaeus were brothers is a real possibility the text never confirms or denies.

As with most of the Twelve, no independent 1st-century source outside the New Testament attests to Matthew's life beyond this calling and his place in the apostle lists.

Cited in: Matthew 9:9; see JAMES SON OF ALPHAEUS.

MATTHEW'S ANTI-PHARISAIC POLEMIC (INTRA-JEWISH CONTEXT, NOT ANTI-JUDAISM)

The scholarly consensus reading of this chapter's harsh, sustained rhetoric against 'the scribes and Pharisees' as reflecting a specific intra-Jewish sectarian conflict between Matthew's own community and a Pharisaic-led Judaism reorganizing itself after the Temple's destruction in 70 CE [319] [320], rather than a timeless theological claim about Jewish people or Judaism as a religion — a distinction mainstream scholarship states explicitly given the chapter's long, documented history of being weaponized in later Christian antisemitism [318] [322] [321]. Compare the same reorganizing-Judaism backdrop behind the Birkat ha-Minim and synagogue-expulsion material in John's Gospel (chapter 9). See also PHARISEES AND SADDUCEES (FIRST-CENTURY JEWISH SECTS) and JERUSALEM.

MILLSTONE (FIRST-CENTURY AGRICULTURAL TECHNOLOGY)

The grinding implement invoked in Jesus's warning that it would be better for an offender of `these little ones'' to be drowned with `a millstone... hanged about his neck'' (18:6). The underlying Greek specifies a mylos onikos, a `donkey millstone'' — the large upper stone of a rotary mill too heavy to turn by hand, requiring an animal yoked to it — a specifically larger and heavier class of object than the small hand-mill or quern a household could operate alone, the kind pictured elsewhere in Matthew's Gospel as two women grinding together (24:41) [271]. Reaching for the largest available class of millstone sharpens the image of a punishment meant to be immediate and irreversible.

MINYAN (PRAYER QUORUM)

The traditional quorum of ten adult Jewish men required, per later rabbinic law, for certain communal acts of worship, including the leader's public repetition of the Shema. The specific number ten is documented with confidence in the Mishnah (compiled around 200 CE, tractate Sanhedrin 1:6) rather than demonstrably fixed already in Jesus's own lifetime. Matthew 18:20's promise that Jesus is present `where two or three are gathered'' in his name specifies a markedly smaller number than the minyan's ten, a real and worth-noting contrast rather than a direct citation or rebuttal of an institution not yet clearly codified at that number in the first century [268]. A separate, earlier Mishnah tradition (Avot 3:2-3) already associates a much smaller gathering of two or three people studying Torah with the resting of the divine presence, a saying structurally close to Jesus's own [268].

MOAB

A kingdom east of the Dead Sea, on a plateau between the Arnon and Zered rivers, in what is now Jordan. Its demonym is Moabite.

Genesis 19:37 traces the Moabites' ancestry to Lot (Abraham's nephew) through an incestuous union with his elder daughter, after the destruction of Sodom — an origin story the text itself frames unflatteringly, not neutrally. Moab and Israel/Judah are frequently hostile in scripture: Numbers 22-24 has the Moabite king Balak hire the prophet Balaam to curse Israel; Deuteronomy 23:3 bars Moabites from the assembly of Israel "even to the tenth generation."

The Mesha Stele (discovered August 1868 by Rev. F. A. Klein at Dhiban, Jordan — biblical Dibon, Moab's capital) is Moab's own royal inscription, erected by King Mesha around 850 BCE. In it, Mesha boasts of his revolt against Israelite domination following the death of Israel's King Ahab — the most important independent, contemporary source for Moab's own political history, told from the Moabite side rather than the biblical one. The stone was smashed by local tribesmen in 1869 in defiance of Ottoman authorities pressuring them to surrender it to Germany; most fragments were later recovered and reassembled, and it is now displayed at the Louvre.

Against this backdrop of scriptural hostility and a real, independently-attested rival kingdom, Ruth — a Moabite woman — becomes King David's great-grandmother (Ruth 4:13-17; Matthew 1:5), placing a member of this same "hostile" nation directly inside the ancestry of Israel's most celebrated king.

Cited in: Matthew (beat covering 1:3-5); see RUTH.

MOSES

Named directly at Matthew 8:4 (Jesus, after healing a leper, tells him to "show yourself to the priest and offer the gift that Moses commanded"), and given rare bodily, on-page presence at the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:1-13), where he appears beside Elijah in a vision witnessed only by Peter, James, and John. Elsewhere Moses functions in Matthew mainly as shorthand for the Law itself; the Transfiguration is the exception, where the text stages him as a living presence rather than a citation.

The archaeological and historical record on a historical Moses and a mass Exodus is, across the range of mainstream biblical scholarship, notably thin to absent. Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman, in *The Bible Unearthed: Archaeology's New Vision of Ancient Israel and the Origin of Its Sacred Texts* (Free Press, 2001) — see their chapter "Did the Exodus Happen?" — argue that decades of excavation across Israel, Sinai, and Egypt have produced no material trace of a large-scale Israelite presence in Egypt, an exodus of the scale Exodus describes, or a subsequent wilderness period, and that the core narrative reads as reflecting the concerns of a much later, seventh-century-BCE audience.

William Dever, in *Who Were the Early Israelites and Where Did They Come From?* (Eerdmans, 2003), argues from decades of his own fieldwork that early "Israel" is better explained as a mostly indigenous Canaanite highland settlement process — roughly 300 small agrarian villages appearing in the central hill country — rather than a foreign population arriving via mass migration. Donald Redford, in *Egypt, Canaan, and Israel in Ancient Times* (Princeton University Press, 1992), surveys the extensive New Kingdom Egyptian administrative record — which tracked corvée labor, foreign slaves, and frontier movement in detail — and finds nothing corresponding to an event of the Exodus narrative's stated scale, proposing instead that the story may derive in part from folk memory of the much earlier expulsion of the Hyksos.

Against this, Kenneth Kitchen's *On the Reliability of the Old Testament* (Eerdmans, 2003) represents the more traditional/maximalist pole of the spectrum, arguing the biblical account remains defensible by analogy to other ancient Near Eastern conventions even where direct Egyptian corroboration is missing. The Merneptah Stele — a granite victory inscription of Pharaoh Merneptah discovered by Flinders Petrie in 1896 at Thebes, dated to roughly 1207 BCE and now in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo — names "Israel" as an already-existing population group in Canaan; it is the earliest and only widely-accepted Egyptian mention of Israel, and is read by many mainstream scholars as evidence for Israel's formation within Canaan rather than an entry into it. No independent source, on any point of this spectrum, names or attests to Moses as an individual historical figure.

The Transfiguration itself sits entirely outside what any of this evidence can check. The scene is private by the text's own account — witnessed only by three disciples, on an unnamed mountain, with no other ancient source claiming independent knowledge of it. The one New Testament passage that explicitly invokes eyewitness testimony to the Transfiguration outside the Synoptic Gospels, 2 Peter 1:16-18 ("we were eyewitnesses of his majesty"), comes from a letter that mainstream critical scholarship regards as pseudonymous and among the latest-written books in the New Testament — see Bart Ehrman, *Forged: Writing in the Name of God* (HarperOne, 2011), chapter 2, on 2 Peter's authorship. Whether Moses and Elijah actually appeared is a theological claim, not a historical one evidence can adjudicate; it is flagged here, not assessed.

Cited in: Matthew (beat covering 8:1-4; beat covering 17:1-13)

MOTHER OF THE SONS OF ZEBEDEE

Never named in Matthew, appearing only by this description: first at 20:20, kneeling before Jesus to ask that her two sons, James and John, sit at his right and left hand in his kingdom, and again at 27:56, watching the crucifixion alongside Mary Magdalene and "the other Mary" (see MARY, MOTHER OF JAMES AND JOSEPH).

Mark's parallel witness-list at the cross (Mark 15:40) names the same group as "Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the less and of Joses, and Salome" — replacing Matthew's unnamed "mother of Zebedee's children" with a named woman, Salome, in the same list position. Comparing the two lists is the entire basis for the common identification of this unnamed mother with Salome; Matthew and Mark are describing the same scene with overlapping but not identical names, and neither Gospel states outright that "the mother of Zebedee's sons" and "Salome" are the same woman. It is a reasonable inference from parallel witness-lists, not a fact either text asserts directly.

Cited in: Matthew 20:20, 27:56; see MARY, MOTHER OF JAMES AND JOSEPH.

MOUNT OF OLIVES

A limestone ridge directly east of Jerusalem's Old City, separated from it by the Kidron Valley, rising slightly higher than the Temple Mount itself. Its identification and geography are not contested in any serious way — it is a real, fixed, easily walkable hill named repeatedly across scripture: David flees over it during Absalom's revolt (2 Samuel 15:30), Zechariah locates a future divine intervention there (Zechariah 14:4), and Acts places Jesus's ascension on it (Acts 1:12). Its slopes have held the region's most prominent Jewish cemetery for well over two thousand years, a practice scholars connect directly to the Zechariah 14 tradition that this is where a final resurrection would begin.

For Matthew, the Mount of Olives is the staging ground the Gospel moves through repeatedly in its final chapters: it is where the donkey is procured for the entry into Jerusalem (21:1), where the Olivet Discourse (see THE TEMPLE) is delivered looking back at the Temple across the valley (24:3), and where Jesus and the disciples go after the Last Supper, on the way to Gethsemane (26:30, 36). None of this geography is in dispute; what is debated, where it arises, concerns specific smaller sites on the mountain's slopes — see BETHPHAGE, BETHANY, and GETHSEMANE.

Cited in: Matthew 21:1; 24:3; 26:30.

MUSTARD SEED (BOTANICAL ACCURACY)

The plant at the center of the parable of Matthew 13:31-32, whose seed Jesus calls the smallest of all seeds. Not literally true across all of nature — orchid and poppy seeds are both smaller — but accurate to the seeds a first-century Galilean farmer would actually have sown as a field or garden crop, among which black mustard was about as small as it got, while the mature plant could grow large enough for birds to nest in its branches [222].

NAPHTALI

The tribe paired with Zebulun in the same Isaiah 9:1–2 / Matthew 4:13–16 fulfillment-quotation, allotted territory in Upper Galilee (Joshua 19:32–39), north and west of the Sea of Galilee toward Hazor. Like Zebulun, "Naphtali" appears as an active combatant people in the Song of Deborah (Judges 5:18) — among the oldest attested Hebrew poetry per Cross and Freedman's dating (see ZEBULUN) — giving the tribal name a plausible claim to real antiquity independent of any later administrative border description.

The Isaiah oracle Matthew quotes was written against the real, externally attested Assyrian conquest of this same region: 2 Kings 15:29 records Tiglath-Pileser III's campaign into Galilee and Gilead and the deportation of the population, an event that correlates with what is independently known from Assyrian royal inscriptions of Tiglath-Pileser III's western campaigns of the 730s BCE, which record subjugating and deporting populations from the northern Israelite kingdom's territory. The Assyrian side of the record does not use the tribal name "Naphtali" itself — that is a biblical, not Assyrian, category — but the conquest event Isaiah's "gloom" and "anguish" describe is not invented; it is the same 8th-century catastrophe known from the Assyrian annals under different administrative vocabulary.

Cited in: Matthew (beat covering 4:13–16); see ZEBULUN.

NAZARETH

A small village in Lower Galilee, unmentioned anywhere in the Hebrew Bible, the Talmud, or Josephus's extensive first-century writings on Galilee — despite Josephus naming dozens of Galilean towns he personally fortified or campaigned near. Matthew 2:23 places Jesus's family there after the return from Egypt, framing it as a fulfillment of unnamed prophetic language ("He shall be called a Nazarene"). John 1:46 preserves a different, unflattering datum: Nathanael's reflexive "Can anything good come out of Nazareth?" — a throwaway line only worth writing down if contemporary audiences actually regarded the place as a nowhere.

The archaeological record backs the "nowhere" reading rather than embarrassing it. In 2009 Yardenna Alexandre, excavating for the Israel Antiquities Authority on a plot adjacent to the Franciscan Church of the Annunciation compound ahead of construction, uncovered the first residential structure from Nazareth's Early Roman-period stratum: a small, modest dwelling with rock-cut walls, along with chalk vessels of the type used by observant Jews of the period to keep food and water ritually pure, and older rock-cut tombs nearby. Alexandre published the full excavation as "The Settlement History of Nazareth in the Iron Age and Early Roman Period" in 'Atiqot 98 (Israel Antiquities Authority, 2020). Her conclusion, echoed in the IAA's original 2009 announcement, is that first-century Nazareth was a poor, out-of-the-way hamlet of perhaps 50 houses on about four acres — not a town of any civic standing.

Nothing in this evidence contradicts Matthew's account of the family living there; it simply confirms that "Nazareth" was exactly the kind of place John 1:46 implies it was, and gives that throwaway line an evidentiary floor it didn't have before 2009.

Cited in: Matthew (beat covering 2:23).

NAZARETH INSCRIPTION

A marble slab inscribed in Greek with an imperial edict — headed diatagma Kaisaros, ordinance of Caesar — forbidding the disturbance of tombs and prescribing a capital charge for removing a buried body. Bought in 1878 by the antiquarian Wilhelm Froehner with a note saying only that it came from Nazareth, and never excavated. For most of the twentieth century it was offered as documentary corroboration of the empty-tomb controversy. In 2020 stable-isotope analysis matched its marble to a quarry on the Greek island of Kos, removing the basis for the Nazareth attribution and suggesting a different occasion entirely: the desecrated tomb of Nikias, a tyrant of Kos. Still a real Roman edict about grave-robbing; no longer evidence about this story.

NETILAT YADAYIM (RITUAL HAND-WASHING)

The later rabbinic name for ritual washing of the hands before eating an ordinary meal, the practice underlying the Pharisees' and scribes' complaint that Jesus's disciples eat with unwashed hands (15:2). At this date the practice is well documented as a Pharisaic extension of priestly-purity thinking to the ordinary table, but mainstream historical-critical scholarship holds it was not yet a universally binding Torah commandment on all first-century Jews — it becomes a fixed, widely codified requirement only in the fuller rabbinic legal tradition of later centuries [239] [240].

NOAH

Noah is invoked briefly, as historical shorthand rather than narrative subject: "as the days of Noah were, so shall also the coming of the Son of man be. For as in the days that were before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day that Noah entered into the ark, and knew not until the flood came, and took them all away" (Matthew 24:37-38) — Noah's flood used as an example of catastrophe arriving without warning into ordinary life.

The flood narrative of Genesis 6-9 is not unique in the ancient Near East; it belongs to a well-documented family of Mesopotamian flood accounts, most famously the flood episode narrated by the immortal survivor Uta-napishti in Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh, and the closely related Atrahasis Epic. See Andrew George, trans., The Epic of Gilgamesh: A New Translation (London: Allen Lane/Penguin Press, 1999), whose introduction discusses the parallels — a global deluge sent to destroy humanity, a single forewarned family preserving life aboard a large boat, birds sent out to test for dry land, and a post-flood sacrifice — as long-recognized points of contact between the Mesopotamian and biblical traditions. Scholars differ on the direction and mechanism of transmission (a common older source, direct literary borrowing during the Babylonian exile, or independent memory of a genuinely catastrophic regional flood), but the existence of the comparative material itself is not in dispute.

None of this bears directly on Matthew's use of the figure, which treats Noah's flood purely as a known reference point for suddenness and unpreparedness, not as a fulfillment-citation requiring its own historicity argument the way Matthew's prophetic quotations do.

Cited in: Matthew 24:37-38.

PAPIAS ACCOUNT OF JUDAS ISCARIOT DEATH (A THIRD TRADITION)

Beyond the contradiction this book's JUDAS ISCARIOT entry already names between Matthew's hanging (27:3-10) and Acts's headlong bursting fall (Acts 1:18), the early-second-century bishop Papias of Hierapolis preserves a third, independently circulating account: Judas surviving for a time in grotesque physical decline before dying, diseased, in his own field [360]. Modern scholarship is divided on whether Papias's account was meant to harmonize Matthew and Acts into one sequence or originally stood as its own separate tradition [361]; the oldest harmonization proposal on record, a rope or branch giving way after the hanging, is laid out directly by F. F. Bruce, who traces it back to Augustine [362]. See PAPIAS OF HIERAPOLIS; JUDAS ISCARIOT.

PAPIAS OF HIERAPOLIS

An early-second-century bishop whose own writings do not survive but are quoted in fragments by the fourth-century historian Eusebius of Caesarea. His testimony that Matthew `collected the sayings in the Hebrew dialect'' is the earliest surviving external claim connecting the name Matthew to any written work, and the starting point — and central complication — for the authorship debate over this Gospel [171]; the fragment's own key terms are themselves disputed among scholars [172]. See GOSPEL AUTHORSHIP (TRADITIONAL ATTRIBUTION VS. CRITICAL SCHOLARSHIP).

PETROS VS. PETRA (PETER/ROCK WORDPLAY)

The Greek wordplay in Matthew 16:18 — "You are Petros [masculine], and on this petra [feminine, "rock"] I will build my church" — that has generated centuries of doctrinal argument over whether Jesus meant Peter himself, or Peter's confession, as the "rock" in view. The linguistic background most mainstream scholars now converge on, across confessional lines, is that Jesus almost certainly spoke Aramaic day to day, in which a single word, kepha, covers both "Peter" and "rock" with no distinction at all [248]; the Greek text's two different forms are best explained as a grammatical necessity (a man's name needs a masculine ending) rather than a deliberate theological distinction [249]. A joint Protestant-Catholic-Lutheran scholarly commission reached this same conclusion while documenting that the verse fueled genuine interconfessional polemic for centuries beforehand [250]. The rock-naming itself is special Matthean material with no parallel in Mark's or Luke's versions of the same scene [251].

PHARISEES AND SADDUCEES (FIRST-CENTURY JEWISH SECTS)

The two Jewish religious-political parties John confronts when he sees them coming to his baptism and calls them a `brood of vipers'' (3:7). The Pharisees emphasized meticulous observance of both the written Torah and an oral tradition of interpretation, along with belief in resurrection and angels; the Sadducees, drawn largely from priestly and aristocratic circles tied to Temple administration, rejected the oral tradition and denied resurrection, and largely disappeared as a group after the Temple's destruction in 70 CE removed the institution their authority depended on. The two groups did not typically make common cause in this period, which is part of why John singling out both together, arriving as a body, has drawn scholarly comment — though nothing in the text explains why they came together on this occasion.

PHILIP (APOSTLE)

Named fifth in Matthew's apostle list (Matthew 10:3) and, per John 1:43-44, from Bethsaida — the same town John gives for Andrew and Peter. He should not be confused with two other New Testament figures sharing his name: Philip the tetrarch (a son of Herod the Great who ruled Iturea and Trachonitis, per the historian Josephus's *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 18), and the "Philip" the Synoptics name as Herodias's first husband before she left him for his half-brother Herod Antipas (Matthew 14:3; Mark 6:17). That second Philip is itself a genuine textual puzzle: Josephus's own account (*Antiquities* 18.5.4) names Herodias's first husband simply "Herod" — a son of Herod the Great by a different wife, Mariamne II, daughter of the high priest Simon — not Philip the tetrarch at all; some translations editorially insert "[Philip]" into that Josephus passage to harmonize it with the Gospels, but the name is not in Josephus's own text at that point. Whether the Gospels erred, or this Herod also carried "Philip" as a second name, is unresolved — and neither candidate is the apostle Philip, a private follower with no political role.

Beyond the call narratives and his brief speaking role in John's Gospel (John 1:45-46, 6:5-7, 12:21-22, 14:8-9), no independent source attests to Philip the apostle's life.

Cited in: Matthew 10:3.

PHILIP (HUSBAND OF HERODIAS)

Named in Matthew 14:3 (and Mark 6:17, Matthew's likely source here) as Herod Antipas's brother and Herodias's first husband, before she left him to marry Antipas. This is very likely a mistaken identification, not a name Josephus — the independent source for the family — ever attaches to Herodias's actual first husband (see HERODIAS).

Herod the Great had at least two sons who could plausibly be meant by "Philip" here, and they were different people. The Philip of Luke 3:1 — "Philip tetrarch of Ituraea and of the region of Trachonitis" — was a son of Herod the Great by Cleopatra of Jerusalem, ruled a separate territory northeast of Galilee for decades (4 BCE–34 CE) with no Gospel controversy attached to him, and, per Josephus (Jewish Antiquities 18.106–108), was known for scrupulous, hands-on local governance — a stable, well-attested, uncontroversial figure. Herodias's actual first husband, per Josephus (Antiquities 18.109), was a different son of Herod the Great — by Mariamne II — referred to by modern scholars as Herod II, who never held any territorial title and is not otherwise prominent in Josephus's account. Because the two men shared a father and the family reused the names "Herod" and "Philip" across multiple sons, most historians read the Gospels' "Philip" here as a conflation of these two distinct half-brothers, rather than evidence that the tetrarch Philip himself was ever Herodias's husband.

Cited in: Matthew 14:3; see HERODIAS.

PHYLACTERIES AND FRINGES (TEFILLIN AND TZITZIT)

Two real, textually commanded Jewish ritual items named in Jesus's charge that the scribes and Pharisees 'make their phylacteries broad and their fringes long' (23:5). Phylacteries (tefillin) are small leather boxes bound to the forehead and arm during prayer, containing four scriptural passages, per a literal reading of Deuteronomy 6:8 and 11:18 [310]; actual first-century examples have been recovered from the Qumran caves [309]. Fringes (tzitzit) are corner tassels with a blue cord, commanded in Numbers 15:38-39 [311], with fringed garments recovered from the later Bar Kokhba-period Cave of Letters extending the material record for the practice across the region [312]. See also PHARISEES AND SADDUCEES (FIRST-CENTURY JEWISH SECTS).

PILATE'S WIFE

Appears once, unnamed, in Matthew 27:19 alone — no other Gospel mentions her — sending Pilate a message during the trial: "Have thou nothing to do with that just man: for I have suffered many things this day in a dream because of him." Matthew gives her no name and no further role.

The name later tradition attaches to her, Procula (and eventually, in the Western church, "Claudia Procula"), first appears in the apocryphal Acts of Pilate, also called the Gospel of Nicodemus (4th–5th century CE), which expands her single dream-warning into a fuller narrative part. A much earlier, unrelated verse — 2 Timothy 4:21, which mentions a Christian named "Claudia" sending greetings — has been read by some in the Eastern church as a reference to this same woman, but the identification is a later inference connecting two otherwise unconnected texts, not a claim either passage makes itself. The Eastern Orthodox and especially Ethiopian Orthodox traditions go furthest, canonizing her alongside her husband (see PONTIUS PILATE) as a saint and martyr, with a feast day in the Ethiopian calendar (June 25) — a tradition resting entirely on the apocryphal material, centuries after the Gospel's single unnamed verse.

Cited in: Matthew 27:19; see PONTIUS PILATE.

PONTIUS PILATE

Prefect of Judea, 26–36 CE, and the Roman official who, per all four Gospels, presided over Jesus's trial and ordered his crucifixion (Matthew 27:2, 11–26). Nothing about his life before this appointment is independently known — no birth record, no attested earlier career — and the "Pontius" name belonged to a known Italian gens (the Samnite Pontii), but no documented family link has ever been established; any specific ancestry proposed for him is speculation, not fact.

The only archaeological find naming him is the Pilate Stone, discovered June 1961 by archaeologist Antonio Frova's excavation team at Caesarea Maritima: a damaged limestone dedication reading "...[Pon]tius Pilatus...[Praef]ectus Iuda[eae]..." It settled a real dispute — later writers including Tacitus (Annals 15.44, c. 116 CE) call him "procurator," a title that only came into use for the province after his tenure; the stone confirms his actual contemporary title was prefect. Independent, non-Christian sources — Josephus (Jewish Antiquities 18.55–89; Jewish War 2.169–177) and Philo of Alexandria (On the Embassy to Gaius, 299–305) — describe a rigid, often violent governor: the "affair of the standards" (nearly suppressing a mass protest after he brought Roman military standards bearing the emperor's image into Jerusalem by night), a deadly riot after he funded an aqueduct from Temple treasury funds, and finally the Samaritan massacre at Mount Gerizim that triggered his recall to Rome, c. 36–37 CE. Mainstream historians (Bond, H. K. (1998). Pontius Pilate in history and interpretation. Cambridge University Press, is the standard monograph) read this independent portrait as directly at odds with the Gospels' increasingly sympathetic, reluctant Pilate — especially Matthew's own addition, the hand-washing gesture (27:24), a Jewish ritual-purification act placed without explanation in a Roman prefect's mouth.

What happened to Pilate after his recall is entirely unknown from any contemporary source; two mutually exclusive later Christian legends — Eusebius's report that he died by suicide in exile (Ecclesiastical History 2.7, 4th century) versus the Coptic and Ethiopian Orthodox traditions that canonized him and his wife as saints (built on the apocryphal Acts of Pilate/Gospel of Nicodemus, 4th–5th century) — are both centuries removed from any contemporary record and served opposite theological needs for the communities that invented them.

Cited in: Matthew 27:2, 11–26, 27:24; see ARCHELAUS, PILATE'S WIFE.

PRAETORIUM

The term Matthew uses (27:27, "governor's headquarters," Greek praitorion) for wherever Pilate was staying in Jerusalem when he had Jesus scourged and handed over for crucifixion — and a genuinely open, still-debated question among scholars and archaeologists as to which building that actually was (see PONTIUS PILATE for the man himself).

Medieval and later Christian tradition — reflected today in the Via Dolorosa pilgrimage route through Jerusalem's Old City — places the trial at the Antonia Fortress, a Herodian-era garrison tower immediately northwest of the Temple Mount. That identification was reinforced in the late 19th and early 20th centuries by the discovery, beneath the Convent of the Sisters of Zion and the nearby Church of the Condemnation, of a large stone-paved plaza (the Lithostrotos) taken to be the "Pavement" of John 19:13. In the 1970s, the French Dominican archaeologist Pierre Benoit demonstrated conclusively that this pavement dates to the 2nd century CE, part of the Emperor Hadrian's rebuilding of Jerusalem as Aelia Capitolina — roughly a century too late to have existed in Pilate's day, undercutting the physical basis for the Antonia identification.

The leading alternative, and the position most mainstream scholarship now favors, places the praetorium instead at Herod the Great's former palace on the city's western hill, near the modern Jaffa Gate and Tower of David. Both Josephus and Philo of Alexandria describe Roman prefects using this palace as their residence and seat of judgment when in Jerusalem for festivals — Philo specifically records Pilate placing votive shields honoring Tiberius there (On the Embassy to Gaius, §299-305; see PONTIUS PILATE) — and note that the Antonia, by contrast, functioned primarily as a military watch-tower over the Temple courts, not as an administrative residence large enough to house a governor's retinue. Archaeologist Shimon Gibson, in The Final Days of Jesus: The Archaeological Evidence (HarperOne, 2009), argues the case in detail from excavated remains of a gate in the palace's western wall, and separately reports raised paving stones near the site, uncovered in 2009, that he proposes as a better candidate for the Gospel's Gabbatha/Pavement than the Hadrianic-era stones under the Antonia.

Neither location is settled beyond dispute, and no inscription or document names the building outright — but the case for Herod's palace, resting on contemporary literary description rather than a pavement now known to postdate the event by a century, is generally regarded as the stronger of the two.

Cited in: Matthew 27:27; see PONTIUS PILATE.

QUEEN OF THE SOUTH / SHEBA

Matthew never uses the name "Sheba"; the figure appears only by title, as "the queen of the south," who "came from the uttermost parts of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon" and who "shall rise up in the judgment with this generation, and shall condemn it," because a generation that will not heed something "greater than Solomon" has failed a test she, from much farther away, passed (Matthew 12:42; parallel Luke 11:31, also using only the title). The identification with the "queen of Sheba" who visits Solomon in 1 Kings 10:1-13 — testing him with hard questions, marveling at his wisdom and wealth, and giving him gold, spices, and precious stones before returning home — is near-universal and not itself contested; what is contested is where "Sheba" actually was.

1 Kings' own text gives no more specific location than the name itself. Two real, independently-attested ancient regions have historically claimed the association: Saba, a wealthy incense-trading civilization in what is now Yemen, attested by its own inscriptions and by excavated temple and irrigation remains at its capital Ma'rib; and Aksum, in the highlands of what is now Ethiopia. The Yemeni identification rests on Saba's well-documented antiquity, trade routes, and geographic fit with a South Arabian spice kingdom "sending" a queen north to Israel. The Ethiopian identification rests almost entirely on the Kebra Nagast ("The Glory of Kings"), an Ethiopian national epic composed in Ge'ez, generally dated by scholars to somewhere between the 6th and 14th centuries CE — many centuries after 1 Kings — which names the queen Makeda, gives her a son by Solomon (Menelik I), and grounds the Solomonic dynasty of Ethiopia's monarchy in that union. See E.A.
