Wallis Budge, trans., The Queen of Sheba and Her Only Son Menyelek: Being the History of the Departure of God and His Ark of the Covenant from Jerusalem to Ethiopia (London: Medici Society, 1922), the standard complete English translation.

The Kebra Nagast is a clean case of legendary accretion built on a spare original: 1 Kings 10 supplies an unnamed queen, an unnamed kingdom, and a visit that ends with her going home; centuries later, the Ethiopian tradition supplies a name, a son, a dynastic founding myth, and a national religious charter, none of which is present in or implied by the biblical account itself. Modern historians generally treat the Kebra Nagast's version as a much later composition serving a specific dynastic-legitimacy purpose for Ethiopia's Solomonic monarchy, rather than as independent historical memory of the 1 Kings event.

Cited in: Matthew 12:42.

QUMRAN / DEAD SEA SCROLLS COMMUNITY

A Jewish sectarian community settled beside the Dead Sea, in the same general wilderness-of-Judea region this chapter locates John's preaching in, active from roughly 100 BCE to 68 CE and responsible for the manuscript library known as the Dead Sea Scrolls, discovered beginning in 1947. Its own initiatory and repeated ritual-washing practice is widely regarded by scholars as the closest attested parallel to John's baptism in the surrounding record, and its Community Rule ties washing explicitly to prior repentance in language often compared to John's own demand for `fruit worthy of repentance'' [94]. Whether John had any personal, direct connection to the community itself remains a genuinely open scholarly question, unresolved in either direction since debate on it began in the 1950s [93].

RAHAB

A prostitute ("zonah," Joshua 2:1) living in the walled city of Jericho (see JERICHO) who shelters two Israelite spies sent ahead of the Israelite advance, hides them from the king of Jericho's men on her roof, and negotiates protection for herself and her family in exchange — marked by a scarlet cord tied in her window (Joshua 2:1-21). When the city falls (Joshua 6, the "walls came tumbling down" episode), Rahab and her household are the one stated exception to the city's destruction, and the text claims her family "dwells in Israel to this day" (Joshua 6:22-25) — an assertion of an ongoing, known descendant line at the time of writing.

Matthew 1:5 goes a step further than Joshua ever does: it makes Rahab the mother of Boaz by a man named Salmon, placing her directly inside the Davidic line, one generation before Ruth marries into the same family. This detail exists nowhere in Joshua or in the book of Ruth itself — Ruth 4:18-22 gives the genealogy from Perez down to David without mentioning Rahab at all, and no other biblical text connects the Jericho Rahab to Salmon or to Boaz. Raymond E. Brown's The Birth of the Messiah (Doubleday, rev. ed. 1993), the standard critical commentary on the infancy narratives, flags this specifically: no other surviving tradition has Rahab marrying Salmon or bearing Boaz, leaving open whether Matthew inherited the detail from a now-lost source or constructed the link himself to complete his patterned genealogy. Working against a purely invented reading, Richard Bauckham's Gospel Women: Studies of the Named Women in the Gospels (Eerdmans, 2002) notes that the Greek forms Matthew uses for Rahab and Boaz diverge from the standard Septuagint spellings used elsewhere in the same list — a small but real textual signal, on Bauckham's reading, that Matthew may be drawing on an independent Jewish genealogical tradition rather than inventing the connection outright. Separately, later rabbinic tradition makes Rahab the wife of Joshua himself, not Salmon — a third, mutually exclusive account of who she married, underscoring that her post-Jericho life was never fixed in a single agreed tradition.

None of this touches Rahab's role inside the Jericho conquest narrative itself, which stands or falls with the historicity question already flagged at JERICHO — a question the Kenyon excavation's redating bears on directly, since Rahab's story requires an inhabited, walled Jericho at the moment of conquest that the site's Late Bronze Age archaeological record does not clearly support.

Cited in: Matthew 1:5; see JERICHO; see RUTH.

RAMAH

A real town in the tribal territory of Benjamin, a few miles north of Jerusalem on the road into the hill country — a common town-name (it simply means "height") not to be confused with other biblical Ramahs. Long associated in tradition with the tomb of Rachel, Jacob's wife and ancestral mother of the tribes of Joseph and Benjamin.

Matthew 2:18 quotes Jeremiah 31:15 to frame Herod's massacre of Bethlehem's infants: "A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation and weeping and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not." In its own original setting the verse has nothing to do with a massacre of infants — it addresses the Babylonian deportation of Israel and Judah in the 6th century BCE. Ramah itself was the real staging point where deportees were assembled before the march to Babylon (Jeremiah 40:1 places the prophet himself there, "bound in chains among all that were carried away captive of Jerusalem and Judah"), and Rachel, buried in the same district, is invoked as the weeping ancestral mother of the exiled tribes personifying national loss — not mourning murdered children. Standard critical commentary on Matthew (W. D. Davies & Dale C. Allison, A Critical and Exegetical Commentary on the Gospel According to Saint Matthew, Vol. 1, T&T Clark, International Critical Commentary, 1988) reads Matthew 2:17-18 as a deliberate later reapplication of Jeremiah's exile-mourning image to an unrelated later event — the same "fulfillment" technique Matthew uses elsewhere with Isaiah 7:14 (see the nativity chronology).

Rachel's tomb location is itself unsettled within scripture: Genesis 35:19-20 places it near Bethlehem/Ephrath, while 1 Samuel 10:2 places it near Zelzah, in Benjamin, in the same district as Ramah — two different traditions, not one consistent site. Some critical readings treat the Bethlehem identification in Genesis as a later addition layered onto an older tradition that originally located the tomb near Ramah, which, if correct, would mean Jeremiah's Ramah/Rachel pairing made straightforward geographic sense on its own terms, independent of the Bethlehem association a reader of Matthew's Gospel might otherwise assume.

Cited in: Matthew 2:18

RANSOM FOR MANY (LYTRON ANTI POLLON)

The Greek phrase (lytron anti pollon) behind Jesus's statement that the Son of Man came `to give his life as a ransom for many'' (20:28). Lytron was an ordinary commercial and legal term in the ancient Mediterranean world for the price paid to free a slave or captive, attested in roughly a thousand manumission inscriptions from Delphi [289] and in Roman law's own formal treatment of ransoming captives from an enemy [290]. The theological interpretation of Jesus's death as such a `ransom'' sits outside what external evidence can confirm or deny; the concrete economic and legal institution the image draws on is real and independently documented.

REGION OF THE GADARENES

The setting of the demon-possession and drowned-swine episode (Matthew 8:28–34) across the Sea of Galilee from Capernaum — and the single most tangled geography problem the Gospel text itself creates. The earliest and best manuscripts of Matthew 8:28 read "Gadarenes"; the earliest and best manuscripts of the parallel accounts at Mark 5:1 and Luke 8:26 read "Gerasenes" instead; a separate manuscript tradition across all three Gospels reads "Gergesenes." These are not spelling variants of one place — they are three different, independently known ancient cities.

Gadara (modern Umm Qais) sits about six miles (roughly 10 km) southeast of the lake — a real, substantially excavated Decapolis city (see DECAPOLIS), but well inland and separated from the shore by a river gorge, not a plausible site for a herd of pigs to stampede "down the steep bank into the sea" as the narrative describes. Gerasa (modern Jerash), another major, extensively excavated Decapolis city, sits roughly 35 miles southeast of the lake — even further away, and effectively impossible as the story's literal setting. Gergesa is the only one of the three that actually sits on the lakeshore itself (identified with modern Kursi, midway along the eastern bank) — but it was a small fishing village, not a walled city, and has the weakest manuscript support of the three readings.

The early Christian scholar Origen already worked through this exact contradiction in his Commentary on the Gospel of John, Book VI, chapter 24 (c. early 3rd century CE), reasoning through the distances by name — ruling out Gerasa as too far, Gadara as still too far, and concluding by elimination that Gergesa, the only shoreline candidate, must be the intended site. Origen reached, by textual and geographic reasoning alone, essentially the same conclusion modern textual critics and archaeologists still favor — roughly 1,800 years before them, using the same method: none of the three named cities sits where the story requires, and the manuscript confusion itself is the oldest evidence that ancient readers already knew it.

Cited in: Matthew (beat covering 8:28); see DECAPOLIS.

RUTH

A Moabite woman (see MOAB) who marries into a Judean family living in Moab during a famine (Ruth 1:1-4), is widowed, and returns to Bethlehem with her mother-in-law Naomi rather than staying with her own people — the central act of loyalty the whole book of Ruth is built around ("where you go, I will go," Ruth 1:16). In Bethlehem she marries Boaz, a kinsman of her late husband's family, through the ancient practice of levirate-adjacent redemption (Ruth 4). Their son Obed is named as the grandfather of Jesse, David's father (Ruth 4:17,21-22) — making Ruth King David's great-grandmother. Matthew's genealogy (1:5) repeats this same line, placing Ruth directly in Jesus's ancestry.

Her foreign origin is not incidental to the story or to Matthew's use of it. Deuteronomy 23:3 bars Moabites from Israel's assembly "even to the tenth generation," and Numbers 22-24 has a Moabite king hire a prophet to curse Israel — scripture's default posture toward Moab, elsewhere, is hostility (see MOAB). The book of Ruth's entire narrative energy comes from a Moabite woman being folded into that same lineage anyway, culminating in the ancestor of Israel's most celebrated king. Matthew including her by name in his genealogy — one of only four women named, alongside Tamar, Rahab, and "the wife of Uriah" — repeats that same move at the start of the New Testament.

Whether Ruth was a historical individual is inseparable from the disputed date and genre of the book that tells her story — see Note 3.

Cited in: Matthew (beat covering 1:3-5); Note 3.

SALOME (TRADITIONAL NAME, NOT IN THE GOSPEL TEXT)

The traditional name attached to the unnamed girl of Matthew 14:6-11 (see DAUGHTER OF HERODIAS), supplied entirely by the independent historian Flavius Josephus rather than by either Gospel. Josephus, in a separate passage describing the wider Herodian family, names Herodias's daughter by her first marriage as Salome and records her own later marriages — first to her step-great-uncle Philip the tetrarch, then after his death to Aristobulus of Chalcis — without ever connecting that Salome to John the Baptist's execution himself [231]. Matthew's own text never supplies a name for the dancer, calling her only "the daughter of Herodias" throughout; the identification with Josephus's Salome is a later inference, built by cross-referencing two of his passages that do not touch each other in his own text, not a reading available from the Gospel's wording itself [232]. The identification is widely regarded as very likely correct, given that Josephus is describing the same family in the same period with no rival candidate on offer, but it remains an inference layered onto the sources rather than something either text states outright.

Cited in: Matthew 14:6-11; see DAUGHTER OF HERODIAS, HERODIAS.

SAMARIA

The hill-country region between Galilee and Judea, named for its capital city (Hebrew Shomron), founded by King Omri of the northern Kingdom of Israel in the early 9th century BCE (1 Kings 16:24). Matthew 10:5 has Jesus instruct the Twelve, on their first mission, to go to "no town of the Samaritans" — carving Samaria out as a third category, distinct from both "the lost sheep of the house of Israel" and the Gentile towns the same verse also forbids. That instruction assumes a real, deep-rooted estrangement rather than inventing one for the scene.

The schism's roots are textually documented centuries before Jesus. Assyria conquered the northern kingdom in 722 BCE and resettled its territory with deportee populations from elsewhere in the empire (2 Kings 17) — the biblical account's own explanation for why Samaritans were regarded as religiously and ethnically compromised. Two centuries later, Nehemiah 2, 4, and 6 record the Persian-appointed governor of Samaria, Sanballat "the Horonite," obstructing and mocking the Judean exiles' rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls and temple (mid-5th century BCE) — a documented, mutual political rupture, not a later literary invention. Samaritans subsequently built their own rival temple on Mount Gerizim, overlooking Shechem.

Independent archaeology both confirms and complicates this. Yitzhak Magen's excavation of the Gerizim precinct (Israel Antiquities Authority, conducted 1983–2003) dated the earliest sacred structure to the mid-5th century BCE — meaning the rival temple went up during, not centuries after, the Judean return, apparently under the same Sanballat family named in Nehemiah. This actually corrects Josephus, whose own account (Antiquities of the Jews, Book 11) places the temple's founding under a different Sanballat roughly two centuries later, during Alexander the Great's conquest. The confusion is resolved by an independent find: the Wadi Daliyeh papyri, a cache of 4th-century BCE Aramaic legal documents and clay seal impressions recovered from a cave north of Jericho in 1962 and analyzed by Frank Moore Cross, which show at least two or three successive Persian-period governors of Samaria all named Sanballat — Josephus, writing centuries later, had apparently telescoped a multi-generation family line into one man.

The Gerizim temple itself stood until the Hasmonean ruler John Hyrcanus I burned it, in a campaign Josephus (Antiquities, Book 13) and most historians date to around 111–110 BCE — a real act of conquest generally treated as the schism's point of no return. Add to this the Samaritans' own scripture, the Samaritan Pentateuch — a Torah text differing from the Jewish Masoretic tradition in thousands of places, including the sectarian core dispute over which mountain God chose — and whose "pre-Samaritan" ancestor text-type is already attested in Dead Sea Scroll fragments by the 2nd century BCE, meaning it is a genuinely ancient rival tradition, not a late medieval fabrication. A destroyed rival temple and a rival Torah, from two independent evidentiary trails, corroborate the estrangement Matthew 10:5 simply takes for granted.

Cited in: Matthew 10:5

SATAN / THE DEVIL / BEELZEBUL

Named as Jesus's tempter in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1-11) and, under the separate name "Beelzebul," accused by Pharisees of being the true source of Jesus's exorcisms (Matthew 12:24 — "It is only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons, that this man casts out demons"). Matthew treats these as the same adversarial figure, but the figure itself has a documented history of change across the centuries separating the Hebrew Bible's earliest uses of the word from the cosmic antagonist Matthew assumes.

In the Hebrew Bible, "satan" (Hebrew ha-satan, "the satan") is a role or title, not a proper name — closer to "the accuser," or "the adversary," a function rather than an individual identity. In Job 1-2 the satan appears among the "sons of God" in the divine council, testing whether Job's loyalty to God would survive hardship; in Zechariah 3:1-2 the satan stands "at the right hand" of the high priest Joshua "to accuse him." In both cases the figure is subordinate to God, performing what reads as an assigned prosecutorial function rather than acting as an independent cosmic enemy. Elaine Pagels traces this evolution in *The Origin of Satan* (Random House, 1995), arguing that the shift from titled function to personalized adversary happens gradually and is substantially a Second Temple-period development, not something already present in Job or Zechariah.

That later, more developed adversary is visible in intertestamental literature the Gospels inherit directly. The Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36), dated by most scholars to roughly the third century BCE, tells of angelic beings ("Watchers") who fall and corrupt humanity — the earliest extended account of this kind. The Book of Jubilees, dated to the second century BCE, introduces Mastema, described as chief of the demons descended from the fallen Watchers, who acts under God's permission to test and tempt humanity; Jubilees 10:11 uses "Mastema" and "satan" interchangeably, functionally merging the two. By the time Matthew was written, this more autonomous, personified adversary — rather than the Hebrew Bible's court-official "accuser" — is the figure available to draw on for the wilderness temptation scene.

"Beelzebul" carries its own separate history. Its root is the Philistine god named at 2 Kings 1:2 as Baal-zebub ("lord of the flies"), worshipped at Ekron. Ugaritic parallel texts (zbl bʿl, "prince, lord") have led a number of scholars to argue the original title was Baal-zebul, "Baal the Prince" or "lord of the exalted house," and that "zebub" ("flies") is a deliberate, satirical corruption by Israelite scribes mocking a rival god's name — though the Masoretic Hebrew text of 2 Kings 1:2 preserves only "zebub." Matthew's Greek form, Beelzeboul, is closer to the "prince" reading than to "lord of the flies," which is part of why the corruption theory has scholarly traction: the New Testament's own spelling doesn't match the mocking version's spelling.

Cited in: Matthew (beat covering 4:1-11; beat covering 12:22-32)

SEA OF GALILEE

A single freshwater lake carrying three different names across the Gospels — no geographic dispute is attached to any of them, only naming convention. Matthew and Mark call it the Sea of Galilee (Matthew 4:18); Luke, using more precise Greek geographic vocabulary for an inland body of water, calls it the Lake of Gennesaret (Luke 5:1); John twice calls it the Sea of Tiberias (John 6:1, 21:1), after the city Herod Antipas founded on its western shore around 20 CE and named for the reigning emperor.

Josephus, writing as a contemporary non-Christian eyewitness with personal command experience in the region during the Jewish revolt, describes the same lake as "the Lake of Gennesareth" in Jewish War 3.10.7–8 (in the Loeb Classical Library edition: Josephus, The Jewish War, Volume II: Books 3–4, H. St. J. Thackeray, Trans., Harvard University Press, 1927), giving its dimensions as 140 by 40 stades — a figure that roughly matches the lake's actual modern measurements of about 21 by 13 kilometers — and describing its shoreline's fishing fleets and the surrounding plain's fertility. This is independent, dated, non-scriptural corroboration of the lake's real existence, location, and character in exactly the period the Gospels describe, with no controversy attached to any of it.

Cited in: Matthew (beat covering 4:18); see GENNESARET.

SEPTUAGINT (GREEK OLD TESTAMENT)

The pre-Christian Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures, produced in stages from roughly the 3rd to the 2nd century BCE, chiefly at Alexandria. New Testament authors writing in Greek, including Matthew, generally quote and rely on this translation rather than working from the Hebrew text directly; the clearest example in this chapter is the fulfillment-quotation of Isaiah 7:14 (1:22-23), where Matthew follows the Septuagint's parthenos ('virgin') rather than the Hebrew almah ('young woman') that Isaiah himself wrote [11]. A Hebrew manuscript predating both the Septuagint's wide circulation among Christians and the New Testament itself confirms the underlying Hebrew wording was already stable centuries earlier [69].

SHAKING OFF DUST (SYMBOLIC ACT)

The gesture Jesus instructs the Twelve to perform against any town that refuses to receive them (10:14): shaking the dust of that place from their feet as they leave. The act repurposes a recognized Jewish practice, codified in the Mishnah, of shaking off the dust of Gentile territory before re-entering the land of Israel, since that dust was treated as conveying the same category of ritual impurity as a grave or corpse [191]. Applied here against a fellow Jewish town rather than Gentile territory, the gesture becomes a pointed act of religious judgment; it is later shown actually being carried out by Paul and Barnabas at Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13:51) [192].

SHAMMAI (RABBINIC SAGE)

A leading Pharisaic sage, contemporary and frequent legal rival of Hillel the Elder, active in Jerusalem in the decades around the turn of the era. The Mishnah remembers his school (Beit Shammai) as consistently reading Jewish law more strictly than Hillel's school (Beit Hillel), including on the specific question of divorce grounds addressed in this chapter: where Hillel's school permitted divorce for almost any dissatisfaction, Shammai's school required an actual 'matter of indecency' [273]. Matthew's Jesus, ruling that divorce is permitted only 'for sexual immorality' (19:9), lands recognizably closer to Shammai's position than to Hillel's [274]. See HILLEL THE ELDER for the general Golden Rule connection already established in this book; the two sages are best read together as opposite ends of a real, live first-century legal spectrum, not as isolated figures.

SIDON

Tyre's sister Phoenician port a short distance up the coast (modern Saida, Lebanon), among the oldest continuously named cities in the ancient Near East — founded by the 3rd millennium BCE and already appearing in Egypt's Amarna letters (mid-14th century BCE) under its then-ruler Zimredda. Matthew 11:21 pairs it with Tyre in Jesus's lament over Chorazin and Bethsaida's unrepentance.

Like Tyre, Sidon's reality is attested across a long, mutually independent documentary record rather than resting on scripture alone: the Amarna correspondence, inscriptions from Ugarit, Homer's Iliad, and Assyrian royal annals all name it. Esarhaddon of Assyria razed Sidon after a 7th-century BCE revolt and refounded it as an Assyrian naval station under a new name meaning "Port of Esarhaddon" — a documented act of imperial punishment and reconstruction, not literary color. The city subsequently passed, in a well-attested political sequence, through Babylonian, Persian, Macedonian (Alexander's conquest), Seleucid, Ptolemaic, and finally Roman control.

As with Tyre, no serious archaeological or historical dispute attaches to whether a real, physically located, Roman-period Sidon existed on the itinerary the Gospels describe (Matthew 11:21, 15:21; Mark 7:24, 31) — the uncertainty that runs through entries like Sodom or the Canaan border lines simply does not apply here. Sidon's ancient archaeological record is, by scholarly consensus, under-excavated relative to its historical importance (systematic modern excavation began only in earnest in the 1990s–2000s and much earlier material was lost to looting and conflict) — a gap in excavation coverage, not a gap in the city's independently documented existence.

Cited in: Matthew 11:21; see TYRE.

SIGN OF JONAH (THREE DAYS AND THREE NIGHTS)

Jesus's only offered `sign' to a crowd demanding proof (12:38-42): as Jonah spent three days and three nights in the great fish, so the Son of Man will spend three days and three nights `in the heart of the earth.' Measured against this same Gospel's own Passion timeline — crucified Friday afternoon, tomb found empty early Sunday morning — the wording claims more than the narrative straightforwardly delivers: parts of three calendar days, but not three literal nights or a full seventy-two hours. The standard harmonization appeals to the ancient Jewish onah convention, in which any part of a day-night unit counts as the whole [212], though even scholars who accept that convention for the `days' generally treat the specific `three nights' as the more strained detail [213] — a genuine, still-discussed internal tension rather than a fully resolved question.

SIMON OF CYRENE

Named at Matthew 27:32 as a man "compelled" by Roman soldiers to carry Jesus's cross toward Golgotha — the Greek verb used, aggareuo, is a Persian loanword denoting the specific Roman legal practice of forcibly conscripting a civilian's labor or transport for military use, and it appears in the New Testament in exactly one other place: Matthew 5:41, in Jesus's own instruction to "go the extra mile" when so compelled, making Simon's conscription a real-world enactment of the very practice Jesus had described earlier in the same Gospel. Cyrene was a genuine Hellenistic city on the coast of North Africa (in modern Libya) with an independently attested, substantial Jewish diaspora community — Acts names a "synagogue of the Cyrenians" active in Jerusalem itself (Acts 6:9) — making Simon's presence in Jerusalem at Passover, as a diaspora Jew likely there for the festival, entirely unremarkable rather than requiring special explanation.

Mark's parallel account (15:21) adds a detail Matthew omits entirely: Simon is "the father of Alexander and Rufus," named as though the Gospel's original audience would recognize them. Paul, writing to the Roman church, sends greetings to "Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine" (Romans 16:13) — a strikingly warm, personal description for an otherwise unremarked-on name. Whether this is the same Rufus, son of the same Simon who carried the cross, is a genuinely intriguing possibility many scholars have floated (it would suggest Simon's family became prominent early Christians, migrating from Cyrene to Rome, with Paul on close personal terms with them) but cannot be confirmed: "Rufus," meaning "red" or "reddish," was itself a common name in the Roman world, including among slaves, and no independent evidence beyond the shared name and Mark's apparent assumption of audience familiarity connects the two passages.

Cited in: Matthew 27:32; Mark 15:21; Romans 16:13.

SIMON PETER

One of four fishermen among the Twelve, called first alongside his brother Andrew (Matthew 4:18-20). His birth name was Simon; "Peter" (Greek *Petros*, "rock") and its Aramaic equivalent "Cephas" (*Kepha*) are both given in scripture as a name Jesus bestowed on him (Matthew 16:18; John 1:42). Paul, writing well before any of the Gospels reached their final form, uses "Cephas" for him consistently (Galatians 1:18, 2:9; 1 Corinthians 1:12, 15:5) — the same identification surfacing independently in the New Testament's earliest surviving strand of evidence, not only in the later narrative Gospels.

Peter is, by a wide margin, the best-attested of the Twelve outside scripture itself. Paul's own letters place him personally in Jerusalem as one of the church's three recognized "pillars," alongside James and John (Galatians 2:9), within roughly two decades of the crucifixion — the earliest independent Christian source for any of the Twelve as a real, active figure. *1 Clement* (a letter from the Roman church, c. 96 CE, still within living memory of the events) references his martyrdom, and Ignatius of Antioch, writing in the early 2nd century, invokes him as an established authority.

The Vatican announced in 1968, under Pope Paul VI, that excavations beneath St. Peter's Basilica (the Vatican necropolis, excavated in stages from the 1940s through the 1960s) had recovered bones judged "consistent with" a man of Peter's approximate age and build. This finding is weaker than its popular reputation: it rests on inference and an unbroken tradition of veneration at that specific spot, not an inscription naming him or any independently verifiable first-century chain of custody, and remains disputed among archaeologists outside the Vatican's own commission.

Cited in: Matthew 4:18; see ANDREW.

SIMON THE CANANAEAN (THE ZEALOT)

Named last but one in Matthew's and Mark's lists as "Simon the Cananaean" (Matthew 10:4; Mark 3:18), and in the same list-position by Luke and Acts as "Simon the Zealot" (Luke 6:15; Acts 1:13) — two epithets that are not actually two different things needing reconciliation, but the same word rendered in two languages. "Cananaean" is not a place-name (it does not mean "from Cana," and does not mean "Canaanite," despite an old and still-repeated mistranslation tradition traced back to the church father Jerome); it transliterates the Aramaic *qanna'*, "zealous one," which the Greek "Zealot" (*zelotes*) simply translates outright. Both Gospel writers are calling him the same thing.

What the label actually meant for a follower of Jesus, sometime before 30 CE, is a genuinely open question rather than a solved one: the organized "Zealot" faction that the historian Josephus names as a distinct militant party did not coalesce as a formal movement until the buildup to the Jewish-Roman War, decades later (66-73 CE). Whether Simon's epithet describes an earlier, less formal zealous temperament or piety, or is a later Gospel-writer's label applied in hindsight from the vocabulary of that later conflict, cannot be settled from the text alone.

Cited in: Matthew 10:4.

SIMON THE LEPER

Named only once, as the host of a dinner in Bethany at which a woman anoints Jesus with costly ointment (Matthew 26:6-13; the parallel appears at Mark 14:3-9). Nothing else is recorded of him — not how or whether he was actually afflicted with a skin disease at the time of the meal (Levitical purity law would have barred an actively "leprous" host from receiving guests at all, which is part of why some readers take the title as describing a past condition, now healed, rather than his present state), nor any connection to Jesus beyond this single scene.

He is one of several men named Simon who appear across the Gospels without being the same person — a genuinely common name in this period and place (see SIMON, BROTHER OF JESUS, on just how common) that produces real identification puzzles: Simon Peter the apostle, Simon the Zealot (another of the Twelve), Simon of Cyrene (see SIMON OF CYRENE), Simon the Pharisee who hosts a broadly similar anointing scene in Luke 7:36-50, and Simon, son of Clopas, named in later tradition. Some readers have proposed that Simon the leper and Simon the Pharisee of Luke 7 are the same host recalled in two different Gospel traditions, since both scenes involve a Simon, a dinner, and a woman anointing Jesus — but the two accounts differ enough in detail (setting, the woman's identity, the disciples' objection) that this identification is a conjecture, not an established fact, and most treatments keep the two Simons distinct.

Cited in: Matthew 26:6-13; see SIMON, BROTHER OF JESUS; SIMON OF CYRENE.

SIMON, BROTHER OF JESUS

The third of Jesus's four named brothers at Matthew 13:55, sharing (per Tal Ilan's Lexicon of Jewish Names in Late Antiquity, Part I: Palestine 330 BCE-200 CE, Mohr Siebeck, 2002) what independent onomastic evidence identifies as the single most common Jewish male name of the era — over 250 individuals named Simon are attested in the surviving Palestinian record from this period alone, which is worth holding in mind whenever a "Simon" appears anywhere else in the Gospels (see SIMON THE LEPER; SIMON OF CYRENE for two of several other, unrelated men sharing this name).

Nothing further is recorded of this Simon in the New Testament or in any independent source: no sayings, no later role, no ossuary, no epistle. Later Christian tradition occasionally identifies him with "Simeon, son of Clopas," a second bishop of Jerusalem named by the 2nd-century writer Hegesippus (as preserved in Eusebius) as James's cousin and successor — a plausible-sounding but not independently verifiable connection resting on nothing more than a shared name and a plausible family relationship.

Cited in: Matthew 13:55; see SIMON THE LEPER; SIMON OF CYRENE.

SODOM

The city Genesis 19 describes God destroying with "sulfur and fire... out of heaven" (19:24), along with Gomorrah (see GOMORRAH) and, per Deuteronomy 29:23, Admah and Zeboiim, for its wickedness — the episode that spares Lot and turns his wife to a pillar of salt. Matthew 10:15 has Jesus invoke Sodom and Gomorrah as the Hebrew Bible's paradigm case of divine judgment, warning that towns which reject his disciples will fare worse "on the day of judgment" than Sodom did.

The leading archaeological candidates for the "cities of the plain" are Bab edh-Dhra and, a few miles south, Numeira — Early Bronze Age town sites on the eastern shore of the southern Dead Sea, in what is now Jordan. Excavated principally by Walter E. Rast and R. Thomas Schaub from 1975 onward (published as Bâb edh-Dhrâ: Excavations at the Town Site (1975–1981), Eisenbrauns, 2003), both sites show genuine, unambiguous violent destruction — burned roof timbers, thick ash layers, collapsed defensive walls — with Numeira's end falling at the close of the Early Bronze III period.

The identification with biblical Sodom remains a real, actively argued proposal, not a settled finding, for one specific reason: the dating does not line up. Rast and Schaub's destruction layers date to roughly 2350–2300 BCE, several centuries earlier than even the most traditional biblical chronologies place Abraham and the Sodom narrative (commonly reckoned around 2000–1900 BCE by straightforward reading of the patriarchal genealogies). No inscription or artifact recovered at either site names the settlement "Sodom." What exists, in other words, is a real, dated, violently destroyed Bronze Age town in roughly the right geography — but not obviously in the right century — which is why mainstream archaeology treats "Bab edh-Dhra is Sodom" as an unproven, if reasonable, hypothesis rather than a confirmed identification, alongside more skeptical readings that treat Genesis 19's cities as unlocatable, composite, or substantially legendary.

Referenced at Matthew 10:15, immediately after the dust-shaking instruction covered in Chapter 10; this book does not separately discuss the Sodom/Gomorrah comparison itself. See GOMORRAH.

SOLOMON

David's son by Bathsheba (see MOAB and RUTH for other women in this same genealogy; Bathsheba is the unnamed "wife of Uriah" of Matthew 1:6), and the son through whom Matthew traces Jesus's line rather than through any of David's other children (1:6) — Luke's competing genealogy instead runs through David's son Nathan (see genealogies-of-jesus.md). 1 Kings 1-11 credits Solomon with succeeding David, building the First Temple in Jerusalem, and an empire and wealth ("wisdom") without precedent in the biblical account — including, by name, fortification work at Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer (1 Kings 9:15).

That verse became the center of a specific archaeological controversy. Excavating at Hazor in 1957-58, Yigael Yadin identified a distinctive six-chambered gate design and, tying it to 1 Kings 9:15, reinterpreted similar structures at Megiddo and a gate at Gezer (previously misread by its original excavator, R. A. S. Macalister, as a much later Maccabean-period structure) as a matched set of "Solomonic" 10th-century royal building projects (Yadin, "Solomon's City Wall and Gate at Gezer," Israel Exploration Journal 8, 1958, pp. 80-86) — for decades treated as one of archaeology's clearest confirmations of a specific biblical building claim.

Israel Finkelstein's "Low Chronology" challenged this directly: reanalyzing the pottery, stratigraphy, and later radiocarbon evidence, Finkelstein argued the same gate-bearing strata actually date roughly a century or more later than Solomon's traditional 10th-century reign — to the 9th-century Omride dynasty (kings Omri and Ahab) of the northern kingdom, not Solomon at all (Finkelstein, "The Archaeology of the United Monarchy: An Alternative View," Levant 28, 1996, pp. 177-187; developed further in Finkelstein & Silberman, David and Solomon, Free Press, 2006). The redating remains actively contested rather than settled in either direction — later radiocarbon work at Gezer has been cited by traditionalist archaeologists as support for the original 10th-century date, while Finkelstein and collaborators continue to defend the Low Chronology in more recent published exchanges — making the Solomon gates one of the more visible ongoing disputes in the wider United Monarchy debate (see DAVID).

Cited in: Matthew 1:6-7.

STAR OF BETHLEHEM

The celestial sign that leads the Magi first to Jerusalem and then to the house where the child is (2:2, 2:9-10). Proposed naturalistic candidates span a rare Jupiter-Saturn conjunction in 7 BCE, a comet recorded in Chinese astronomical annals in 5 BCE [75], and a lunar occultation of Jupiter in 6 BCE (see note 12, earlier in this chapter); a substantial body of scholarship argues instead that the star is a literary device drawing on Numbers 24:17's messianic `star out of Jacob'' rather than a claim about an observed astronomical event [77], and a full skeptical survey finds none of the naturalistic candidates matching the text's description of a star that moves ahead of travelers and stops over a single house [76].

SUFFERING SERVANT (ISAIAH 53) — MATTHEW'S HEALING APPLICATION

The unnamed servant figure of Isaiah 52:13-53:12, quoted in this chapter at Matthew 8:17 ('he took our illnesses and bore our diseases,' from Isaiah 53:4) as the explanation for Jesus's healing activity just narrated. Matthew's application here is to physical healing alone, with no reference to vicarious suffering for sin [163] — a narrower reading than the vicarious-atonement sense the same passage (especially Isaiah 53:5) takes on elsewhere in the New Testament, and the citation's placement is generally read as Matthew's own editorial framing rather than an inherited detail [164]. See ISAIAH for the prophet and GREAT ISAIAH SCROLL (1QISA^A) for the manuscript tradition.

SYRIA

The large Roman province directly north of Judea, governed by an imperial legate of consular rank — a senior posting, reflecting Syria's importance as a frontier province with its own permanently stationed legions. Matthew 4:24 mentions Jesus's reputation spreading "throughout all Syria" as a simple geographic notice of his fame reaching beyond Galilee's own borders.

Syria's legate held real oversight relevance for the smaller territories to its south, including Judea, particularly at moments of direct annexation. Publius Sulpicius Quirinius, serving as legate of Syria, conducted a census of Judea in 6 CE at the moment of its annexation as a Roman province following Archelaus's deposal — a real, independently dated event recorded by Josephus (Jewish Antiquities 18.1.1) and cross-referenced by Luke's own later book (Acts 5:37). Luke's Gospel (2:1-2) places a Quirinius census at Jesus's birth instead, under Herod, roughly a decade earlier than the attested 6 CE census — a chronology gap addressed in full in the nativity chronology topic document, not here. This entry notes only that the underlying Syria-Judea administrative relationship Luke's detail depends on — a Syrian legate with real authority to order a Judean census — is itself well attested (Fergus Millar, The Roman Near East, 31 BC-AD 337, Harvard University Press, 1993), independent of the separate dating problem.

Cited in: Matthew 4:24

TALENT (ANCIENT CURRENCY UNIT)

The largest unit of ancient Mediterranean currency reckoning, equivalent to roughly six thousand denarii — and a denarius was the standard attested daily wage for an ordinary hired laborer in the early Roman world [269]. The parable of the unforgiving servant (18:23-35) hinges its entire argument on this real exchange rate: a debt of ten thousand talents comes to tens of thousands of years of ordinary wages, more than sixteen times the six-hundred-talent annual tribute Judea, Samaria, and Idumea together owed Rome under Herod's son Archelaus [270] — a deliberately impossible sum set beside the fellow servant's realistic, modest debt of a hundred denarii, about three months' wages.

TALENT PARABLE (ANCIENT BANKING CONTEXT)

The parable of a master entrusting three servants with five, two, and one talent respectively before a journey (25:14-30; see TALENT (ANCIENT CURRENCY UNIT) for the sum itself). Its economic logic rests on two real, attested ancient practices: professional bankers (trapezitai) who took deposits and paid interest were a genuine, ordinary commercial option [341], while burying an entrusted deposit was, under rabbinic legal tradition, the maximally cautious, liability-clearing method of safekeeping available to a custodian [342]. Luke preserves an independent version of the same core story at a different scale, the parable of the ten minas (Luke 19:11-27) [343].

TAMAR

A woman who marries two of Judah's sons in succession, Er and Onan, both of whom die before providing her an heir (Genesis 38:6-10). Judah, fearing the loss of his one remaining son, withholds the youngest, Shelah, from the levirate obligation owed to her (38:11) — a promise the narrative makes clear he never intends to keep. When Tamar recognizes she has been denied what custom owed her, she disguises herself as a roadside prostitute and conceives by Judah himself without his knowledge (38:13-19), later proving the child is his by producing his own seal, cord, and staff, left with her as a pledge (38:24-26). Judah's response is not condemnation but the reverse: "She is more righteous than I, since I did not give her to my son Shelah" (38:26). Her own ethnic origin is never stated directly; Genesis 38:1-2 places her inside a household Judah built after he "went down" among Canaanites and took a Canaanite wife for himself, and later tradition often assumes Tamar herself was Canaanite, though the text itself does not say so. The twins she bears, Perez and Zerah, become the eponymous ancestors of two Judahite clans named in the wilderness census (Numbers 26:20-21); Perez's line runs forward through Ruth 4:18-22 to David, and from there into Matthew's genealogy (1:3).

Read purely as family drama, Genesis 38 is a self-contained episode that interrupts the surrounding Joseph narrative — chapter 37 ends with Joseph sold into slavery in Egypt, chapter 39 resumes exactly there, with chapter 38 sitting between them as its own unit. E. A. Speiser's Anchor Bible commentary, Genesis (Doubleday & Company, 1964), reads the underlying material as tribal history as much as personal biography: the Judahite line is, in the story's own terms, at risk of dying out until Tamar's action secures it, and its center of gravity may be less "what Tamar did" than an origin account for why the Perezite clan outranked the older Zerahite one within the tribe of Judah — the twins' birth itself is staged as a contest (38:27-30), Zerah's hand emerging first before Perez pushes past him to be born, a detail read as a just-so account of the younger clan's eventual precedence.

Matthew names Tamar directly rather than passing over her, the same choice he makes for Rahab and Ruth and pointedly does not make for Bathsheba (see BATHSHEBA) — four women, each attached to a sexually irregular or scandalous circumstance, three of them also foreign or foreign-adjacent by birth or marriage into a non-Israelite household. Whether that pattern was deliberate on Matthew's part is not something this entry adjudicates, but it recurs too consistently across four consecutive names to be coincidence.

Cited in: Matthew 1:3; see RUTH.

TAX COLLECTORS (TELONAI) IN ROMAN JUDEA

Local toll and tax collectors, called telonai in Greek, who purchased collection contracts from Roman or, in Galilee specifically, Herodian authorities and recouped their investment, plus profit, by collecting above the contracted rate from their own communities. Beyond that economic resentment, tax collectors were also widely treated in the period's literature as functionally assimilated toward Gentile status, since the work required routine handling of Gentile coinage and regular commercial dealing with Gentiles on Gentile terms — a boundary-marking exclusion distinct from unpopularity alone [177], though some scholars weight the underlying offense differently, as a moral rather than a purely social-boundary category [178]. This is the social world invoked when Matthew draws criticism for eating with `tax collectors and sinners'' after his calling (9:9-11; see MATTHEW (LEVI)).

TEMPLE TAX / DIDRACHMA (FISCUS JUDAICUS POSTSCRIPT)

The annual half-shekel (didrachma) levy on adult Jewish men described in Matthew 17:24-27, rooted in the census-ransom law of Exodus 30:11-16 [262] and collected not only in Judea but from Jewish communities across the Mediterranean diaspora, a reach independently attested by Philo and by Cicero's Pro Flacco [263]. The tax had to be paid in Tyrian shekels [45], and its later history is itself a documented postscript: after the Temple's destruction in 70 CE, Vespasian redirected the same sum, still collected empire-wide, to fund Rome's Temple of Jupiter instead, a policy known as the Fiscus Judaicus and later enforced with particular severity under Domitian [41].

TEN VIRGINS / BRIDESMAIDS (FIRST-CENTURY WEDDING CUSTOM)

The ten young women who wait for a bridegroom's arrival to begin a wedding procession (25:1-13), five prepared with extra oil for a long wait and five not. The scenario reflects genuine first-century village wedding practice: a groom's actual arrival time was not fixed in advance and could run past midnight, a real, unpredictable feature of the custom rather than an invented plot device built solely to argue for vigilance [339] [340].

TESTAMENT OF ISSACHAR (TESTAMENTS OF THE TWELVE PATRIARCHS)

A section of the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, a Jewish pseudepigraphal work (with debated Christian interpolations and compositional history) presenting Jacob's twelve sons delivering farewell instructions to their descendants. Issachar's testament pairs love of God with love of neighbor twice (5:2; 7:6), independently attesting the same two-commandment summary of the Law that Jesus gives at Matthew 22:37-40 [306].

THADDAEUS

The name given to the tenth apostle in Matthew 10:3 and Mark 3:18 — and the clearest case among the Twelve of the same person appearing under openly different names across the New Testament's own texts, with no acknowledgment anywhere that a discrepancy exists. Some manuscripts of Matthew read "Lebbaeus" instead of "Thaddaeus" at this exact point (a manuscript-tradition variant, not an easily explained scribal accident). Luke's list and Acts both drop "Thaddaeus" entirely and instead give "Judas son of James" in the same list-position (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13). John's Gospel, separately, has a disciple ask a question at the Last Supper introduced as "Judas (not Iscariot)" (John 14:22) — almost certainly the same figure again, distinguished specifically from Judas Iscariot (see JUDAS ISCARIOT) because the shared first name Judas was common enough to need the clarification.

Three names — Thaddaeus, Lebbaeus, Judas son of James — for, in all likelihood, one man, with a fourth Gospel using a fifth descriptive phrase for what is probably the same person again. No text anywhere reconciles the naming; readers are left to make the identification themselves, exactly as with Bartholomew/Nathanael and Matthew/Levi elsewhere on this list.

Cited in: Matthew 10:3; see JUDAS ISCARIOT.

THE JEREMIAH ATTRIBUTION: CANONICAL ORDER AND THE CHURCH FATHERS (MATTHEW 27:9-10)

Supplementary background to this book's JEREMIAH entry, which already lays out the basic composite-citation problem at 27:9-10. Two further explanations circulate in modern scholarship: that Jeremiah headed a collected unit of the Latter Prophets in some canonical orderings (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 14b), making a citation from within that unit nameable after its lead book [357]; and Robert Gundry's dissenting view that Matthew is not quoting Jeremiah at all but presenting the chief priests' actions as a typological reenactment of Jeremiah's potter-and-field narratives, with Zechariah supplying only the wording [358]. The puzzle is also ancient rather than modern: Augustine and Jerome both addressed it directly in the fourth and fifth centuries, with Jerome reporting — without vouching for it himself — a Hebrew writing attributed to Jeremiah that a Nazarene sect member showed him, containing wording close to Matthew's own [359].

THE LEAST OF THESE (INTERPRETIVE DEBATE)

The phrase used twice in the sheep-and-goats judgment scene (25:40, 45) to describe who the righteous fed, clothed, and visited. Whether it means all of suffering humanity or specifically Jesus's own missionary disciples (his 'brothers' in this Gospel's narrower, repeated sense of the word) is a genuinely open question with a long interpretive history, not a settled one [346] [347].

THE MAGI (WISE MEN)

Unnamed, uncounted visitors from `the East'' who come to Jerusalem asking after a newborn king of the Jews, guided by a star, and who present the infant Jesus with gold, frankincense, and myrrh before being warned in a dream not to return to Herod (2:1-12). `Magi'' (Greek magoi) denotes a recognized class of Persian or Babylonian priest-astrologers, not royalty. Matthew gives no number of visitors and no names; both the traditional count of three and the later names Melchior, Caspar, and Balthasar are demonstrably later accretions, the names first attested roughly five centuries after this Gospel [79], and their royal status a still-later typological reading of Psalm 72 and Isaiah 60 [80].

THE TEMPLE

The building Matthew's Jesus enters and overturns tables in (21:12) is formally the Second Temple — the structure rebuilt after the Babylonian exile — but in the physical sense it was a wholly different, far larger building, the product of a massive rebuilding and expansion project Herod the Great began in the eighteenth year of his reign, conventionally dated to about 20-19 BCE (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 15.380). Herod's engineers roughly doubled the platform of the Temple Mount to some 36 acres and encased it in new retaining walls, the lower courses of which survive today — including the western section now known as the Western Wall (the "Wailing Wall"), which is a retaining wall for the platform itself, not a wall of the sanctuary building it once supported. Josephus, who had seen the building standing as a young priest before its destruction, left the most detailed surviving architectural description of any comparable ancient structure (Jewish War 5.184-247), describing white stone and gold facing visible, he claims, from a considerable distance. Construction and expansion work continued for roughly eighty years without ever closing the Temple to worship, meaning the building Matthew's Jesus disrupts was still, technically, an active construction site.

Titus's forces destroyed it during the siege of Jerusalem in August of 70 CE; Josephus records the burning of the sanctuary in detail (Jewish War, Book 6). His account also supplies an unglamorous, non-supernatural mechanism for the specific claim, put in Jesus's mouth, that "not one stone will be left here upon another" (Matthew 24:2): the building's gold facing melted in the fire and ran into the cracks between its foundation stones, and Roman soldiers subsequently pried the stones apart hunting for it — a literal fulfillment driven by looting, not prophecy fulfilling itself unaided.

That destruction matters for more than architecture — it bears directly on when Matthew itself was written. Raymond E. Brown's standard scholarly survey, An Introduction to the New Testament (Doubleday, 1997), summarizes the mainstream historical-critical position: most scholars place Mark's composition in the late 60s CE, with the Jewish War against Rome already underway but Jerusalem's fall not yet accomplished, and a growing minority placing it just after 70; Matthew, written later and using Mark as a source, is placed by the same mainstream consensus in the 80s CE, safely after the Temple's actual destruction. On this reading, Matthew's version of the Olivet Discourse (ch. 24, expanding Mark 13) reflects an author who already knew how the story of the Temple ended — a case of the narrative's own claimed foreknowledge being written with the benefit of hindsight, a pattern scholars in this field call vaticinium ex eventu ("prophecy after the fact").

Cited in: Matthew 21:12; 24:1-2.

THE TWELVE APOSTLES (LIST VARIANCE ACROSS SOURCES)

The general term for the inner circle of twelve men Jesus commissions in this chapter (10:1-4), independently listed four times across the New Testament (Matthew 10:2-4, Mark 3:16-19, Luke 6:14-16, Acts 1:13). The four lists agree on the great majority of names and on a consistent three-tier grouping structure, but disagree at the tenth name — Thaddaeus in Matthew and Mark, Judas son of James in Luke and Acts — with a further manuscript variant reading Lebbaeus for Thaddaeus in some copies of Matthew [186] [187]. The standard reading treats the two names as one apostle under two designations, though nothing in the text itself confirms this beyond inference.

THIRTY PIECES OF SILVER (ZECHARIAH 11:12-13 CITATION)

The price Judas accepts from the chief priests to betray Jesus (26:15), matching Zechariah 11:12-13's account of a rejected shepherd's wages cast into the Temple treasury [349], and independently echoing Exodus 21:32's legal price for a slave gored to death by an ox [350]. Matthew does not cite Zechariah by name at this point in the narrative; the Gospel's explicit citation of the related material, misattributed to "Jeremiah," comes later, when the money resurfaces at 27:9-10.

THIS GENERATION (MATTHEW 24:34 INTERPRETIVE CRUX)

The closing claim of the Olivet discourse's first half, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place (24:34), turns on what Matthew's Greek genea, generation, means here. A straightforward reading ties the described events to the lifespan of Jesus's own contemporaries, a horizon the actual fall of Jerusalem in 70 CE satisfies precisely [334]. Other readings take genea in a qualitative sense, a generation or kind of people, or propose the verse originally covered only the near-term signs of verses 4-28 while the cosmic imagery of verses 29-31 addresses a separate, later horizon [335]. The crux remains genuinely open and is argued in earnest across the confessional spectrum of Matthew's interpreters, not a settled question with an agreed answer.

THOMAS

Named in all four lists (Matthew 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:15; Acts 1:13); John's Gospel three times glosses him as "Thomas, called Didymus" (John 11:16, 20:24, 21:2). This is not two names but one meaning stated twice: "Thomas" is itself Aramaic for "twin" (*te'oma*), and "Didymus" is simply its Greek translation — John is telling the reader what the Aramaic name already means, not supplying an additional nickname. Whose twin he was is never stated.

Thomas carries the strongest non-canonical secondary tradition of any apostle besides Peter. The apocryphal *Acts of Thomas* (a 3rd-century Syriac composition) claims he traveled to India, and the Saint Thomas Christian community of Kerala, in southern India, maintains a continuous tradition tracing its founding to him down to the present day — documented in historian Robert Eric Frykenberg's 2008 history *Christianity in India: From Beginnings to the Present* (Oxford University Press). This tradition deserves more weight than most apostolic legends, because the underlying possibility is genuinely plausible — an active Indo-Roman trade route via the Malabar pepper coast operated in the 1st century CE — but the *Acts of Thomas* itself is still a later, centuries-removed hagiographical composition, not a contemporary attestation of the events it narrates.

Cited in: Matthew 10:3.

THREE GIFTS (GOLD, FRANKINCENSE, MYRRH)

The Magi's presentation gifts to the infant Jesus (2:11), and the sole textual basis for the popular tradition of `three'' wise men — Matthew names three gifts, never a number of visitors. Frankincense and myrrh were genuine high-value commodities of the period, harvested in southern Arabia and carried to the Mediterranean along a single long-distance caravan route [78]; gold needs no such explanation, being a universal ancient luxury good. The gifts' real economic grounding stands in contrast to everything later ages built on top of them — a specific count of visitors, names, and royal status — none of which the text itself supplies.

TRANSFIGURATION (MOSES/ELIJAH TYPOLOGY)

The mountain scene of Matthew 17:1-8 in which Jesus's appearance changes before Peter, James, and John, and Moses and Elijah appear speaking with him. The scene's cloud, glory, and voice-from-the-cloud imagery is built out of Moses's own Sinai encounters (Exodus 24:15-18; 34:29-35) [256], while Elijah's presence recalls his matching theophany at Horeb (1 Kings 19:8-13) [257]; together the two figures stage Matthew's own recurring phrase 'the Law and the Prophets' (Matthew 5:17; 7:12) [258] as an on-page tableau. The chapter's unusually precise 'after six days' opening (17:1) is itself read as a further echo of Exodus 24:16's own six-day interval before Moses is called into the cloud [259]. See also MOSES and ELIJAH for the figures individually.

TRIBUTE PENNY (TIBERIUS DENARIUS)

The silver denarius Jesus requests in the render-unto-Caesar exchange (22:19-21), identified by numismatists as a coin struck under Tiberius. Its obverse carries the emperor's portrait ringed by TI CAESAR DIVI AVG F AVGVSTVS, a minted claim to divine sonship [46]; its reverse carries a seated figure generally identified as Livia personified as the goddess Pax, ringed by the legend PONTIF MAXIM, Tiberius's title as Rome's chief priest [304]. See also the DENARIUS (ROMAN DAY-LABORER WAGE) entry (chapter 20), which covers the same coin denomination's ordinary wage value rather than this specific type's inscriptions.

TYRE

A Phoenician port city on the coast of what is now Lebanon, and — unlike most Gospel place-names touched on so far — one whose existence, location, and major historical events are independently and extensively documented across more than a thousand years, well before any scriptural mention. Matthew 11:21 has Jesus lament that Tyre and Sidon (see SIDON), pagan cities by any traditional reckoning, would have repented in sackcloth and ashes had they witnessed the miracles done in Chorazin and Bethsaida.

Assyrian royal annals record repeated campaigns against Tyre under Shalmaneser V and Sargon II (c. 724–720 BCE), Sennacherib (701 BCE), Esarhaddon (671 BCE), and Ashurbanipal (663 BCE) — the city's island fortifications withstood them all. Egypt's Amarna letters (mid-14th century BCE diplomatic correspondence) already list Tyre among the Levantine vassal city-states reporting to Pharaoh. Centuries later, Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon besieged the mainland city for a traditional thirteen years (commonly dated c. 586–573 BCE); Josephus preserves this detail in Against Apion, Book 1, by quoting the Hellenistic historian Menander of Ephesus's now-lost history of Tyre — itself, Menander says, drawn from Tyre's own royal archives — naming the Tyrian king of the day as Ithobal. That is an independent chain of transmission (Tyrian court record → Menander → Josephus) confirming the siege from the Phoenician side, separate from the biblical prophetic tradition that also describes it (Ezekiel 26–29).

Alexander the Great's seven-month siege of the island city in 332 BCE ended Tyre's independence for good; per the Greek historian Diodorus Siculus (Bibliotheca Historica, Book 17), Alexander built a causeway from the mainland to the island using rubble that included stone from the mainland city Nebuchadnezzar had razed generations earlier. Taken together, this is a case where the Gospel place-name sits on essentially uncontested ground — Assyrian, Egyptian, Babylonian, and Greek sources, produced by mutually unrelated and often hostile political traditions, agree that Tyre was a real, continuously identifiable city exactly where later Gospel geography (Matthew 15:21 has Jesus travel to "the district of Tyre and Sidon") places it.

Cited in: Matthew 11:21; see SIDON.

TZARAAT / LEPRA (ANCIENT SKIN-DISEASE CATEGORIES)

The Hebrew term applied to the skin condition healed in this chapter's opening scene (8:1-4), rendered lepra in the Septuagint and Greek New Testament and 'leprosy' in most English translations. Modern medical and historical scholarship distinguishes tzaraat/lepra as a broad priestly diagnostic category covering a range of skin, hair, and even fabric or wall conditions, from the single, specific modern disease Hansen's disease (caused by Mycobacterium leprae) [156]. Leviticus 13-14 lays out the priest's own detailed, non-medical certification procedure for the category [157]. See also REGION OF THE GADARENES for a comparable case where a single Gospel term maps imperfectly onto a modern category.

VATICINIUM EX EVENTU (PROPHECY AFTER THE FACT)

Latin for prophecy from the outcome: a recognized ancient literary device in which a text places words of prediction in the mouth of an earlier narrator or prophet, describing, often in precise detail, events that had already occurred by the time the text was actually composed. Daniel 10-12 is the textbook biblical example, accurate in fine detail through the reign of Antiochus IV Epiphanes, then wrong about his death, the seam scholars use to date Daniel's actual composition to the 160s BCE [329]. The majority critical reading of this chapter's Olivet discourse treats it as a New Testament instance of the same device, sharpening a shorter saying of Jesus into the specific shape the Jewish War of 66-70 CE actually took [330]; a minority of conservative and evangelical scholars dissent, arguing the specificity does not require after-the-fact composition [331].

VIA MARIS

The region's principal north-south trade route in antiquity, linking Damascus to the Mediterranean coast and passing directly through Capernaum on the Sea of Galilee's northwest shore. Capernaum's position on this route, and on the border between Herod Antipas's Galilee and Herod Philip's territory, is the historical-economic backdrop to Jesus settling there in this chapter (4:13) and to Matthew's own later scene of a toll collector working at the same town (Matthew 9:9) [106].

WICKED TENANTS (PSALM 118 / REJECTED STONE)

The parable of the vineyard tenants who kill the owner's son (21:33-46), closing on Jesus's citation of Psalm 118:22-23, 'the stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone' (21:42). A dedicated monograph on this parable argues the stone citation belongs to its earliest layer, tied to the rejected-son plot by a Hebrew/Aramaic sound-play between 'son' (ben) and 'stone' (eben) [301]. The same verse is independently cited in Mark 12:10-11, Luke 20:17, Acts 4:11, and 1 Peter 2:7, making it one of the most frequently reused single verses in early Christian messianic proof-texting [302].

WILDERNESS OF JUDEA

A real, geographically uncontested arid region east of the Judean hill country, descending toward the Dead Sea — the setting Matthew 3:1 gives for John the Baptist's preaching. Its location and general character are not in dispute.

Within this same wilderness, roughly one to two miles from the Dead Sea's western shore, sits Qumran, the site of a Jewish sectarian settlement (2nd century BCE–68 CE) whose scrolls and material culture are usually associated with the Essenes, per Josephus, Philo, and Pliny the Elder's descriptions of that group. The genuine geographic overlap between John's traditional preaching ground and Qumran's location, plus shared elements — both used Isaiah 40:3's "a voice crying in the wilderness" as self-description, and both practiced ritual immersion — has led many New Testament scholars to propose some connection between John and the Essene movement.

That proposed connection remains speculative, not established. Joan E. Taylor's The Immerser: John the Baptist within Second Temple Judaism (Eerdmans, 1997) examines the parallels directly and concludes the differences between John's practice and Qumran's outweigh the similarities — that any contact, if it occurred, would most plausibly have been with urban Essenes rather than the Qumran community itself, and that John is better understood as an independent figure than as a product of, or convert from, the Qumran sect. The geography is real and adjacent; the institutional link is not confirmed.

Cited in: Matthew (beat covering 3:1).

WOE ORACLE (PROPHETIC RHETORICAL FORM)

A recognized unit of Hebrew prophetic speech (Hebrew hoy), built from a formulaic opening exclamation followed by an indictment and often a threatened consequence [313]. Isaiah stacks six such woes against specific social sins in a single sequence (Isaiah 5:8-23), and Habakkuk gathers five more into one taunt-song (Habakkuk 2:6-19) [314]. Matthew's sevenfold 'woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites' (23:13-36) is read by mainstream critical commentary as a deliberate adoption of this same inherited prophetic form, not an invented mode of attack [315].

YOKE OF THE TORAH / KINGDOM OF HEAVEN (RABBINIC METAPHOR)

The Jewish idiom, attested in the Mishnah, of describing religious obligation itself as a 'yoke' voluntarily taken up: reciting the Shema is framed as first accepting 'the yoke of the kingdom of heaven' and then 'the yoke of the commandments' (m. Berakhot 2:2) [204], while a separate saying attributed to Nehunya ben ha-Kanah holds that taking on 'the yoke of the Torah' removes the yoke of government and worldly cares (m. Avot 3:5) [205]. Both Mishnaic formulations postdate the Gospels by a century or more in their written form, but they document a durable image already available in the wider Second Temple and early rabbinic world — the same image Matthew's Jesus uses when inviting hearers to 'take my yoke upon you' at 11:29-30, and which Ben Sira's Wisdom figure uses in nearly the same sequence two centuries earlier (Sirach 51:23-27) [206].

Cited in: Matthew (beat covering 11:28-30).

ZEBEDEE

A Galilean fisherman, father of the apostles James and John (see JAMES SON OF ZEBEDEE, JOHN SON OF ZEBEDEE), named only in the call narrative with no independent action of his own anywhere in the New Testament. Mark 1:19-20 describes him left in the boat "with the hired servants" when his sons leave to follow Jesus — a small detail worth noting because it implies a fishing operation large enough to employ paid labor beyond the family itself. Mendel Nun, a lifelong Sea of Galilee fisherman based at Kibbutz Ein Gev who spent decades documenting the lake's ancient fishing methods, reconstructed 1st-century Galilean fishing as commonly organized around multi-man crews and boat-owning households of roughly this scale, consistent with a boat needing more hands than two sons alone.

Comparing Matthew 27:56 ("the mother of the sons of Zebedee") with Mark 15:40 (which names a "Salome" in the same list of women at the crucifixion) is the basis for the common identification of Zebedee's wife as Salome — a reasonable harmonization across two independent Gospel accounts, but not something either text states on its own. This is a different Salome from Herodias's dancing daughter in Matthew 14:6-11.

Beyond his name, occupation, and boat, nothing about Zebedee survives in any source, scriptural or otherwise.

Cited in: Matthew 4:21; see JAMES SON OF ZEBEDEE, JOHN SON OF ZEBEDEE.

ZEBULUN

One of the twelve tribes of Israel, allotted territory in interior Lower Galilee under Joshua 19:10–16 — inland, west of the Sea of Galilee, in the same general area that later includes Nazareth. Matthew 4:13–16 quotes Isaiah 9:1–2 as being fulfilled by Jesus's move to Capernaum, "in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali" — but Isaiah's oracle originally addressed the actual historical Assyrian conquest of Galilee under Tiglath-Pileser III around 732 BCE (2 Kings 15:29), some 750 years before Matthew's use of it. Matthew keeps Isaiah's place names while repurposing the "gloom to light" structure of the original oracle for an entirely different, later event.

Independent of any external inscription, "Zebulun" appears as a named, active fighting people in the Song of Deborah (Judges 5:14, 18), which orthographic and morphological analysis by Frank Moore Cross and David Noel Freedman ("Early Yahwistic Poetry") places among the oldest surviving Hebrew poetry, likely composed close to the 12th–11th century BCE events it describes — genuine evidence the tribal name is old, even though (as with Canaan generally) no outside source independently fixes Zebulun's borders the way Numbers 34 or Joshua 19 describe them.

Cited in: Matthew (beat covering 4:13–16); see NAPHTALI.

ZECHARIAH 9:9 (TWO-ANIMAL MISREADING)

The prophetic verse Matthew cites for the Triumphal Entry (21:5), 'humble, and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey' — Hebrew synonymous parallelism naming one animal twice [293]. Matthew alone stages the scene with two literal animals, a doubling read by the mainstream critical commentary tradition as a literalized misreading of the poetic form rather than a separately intended detail [294].

ZECHARIAH, SON OF BARACHIAH

Named once, in a list of righteous blood shed "from the blood of righteous Abel unto the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom ye slew between the temple and the altar" (Matthew 23:35) — Jesus's summary indictment spanning the entire Hebrew canon from its first murder to (implicitly) its last. Luke's parallel (11:51) repeats the same "Zechariah" and the same location but drops the patronymic entirely, naming only "Zechariah," who perished between the altar and the temple.

The patronymic creates a genuine identification problem that commentators have never fully resolved. Two candidates compete: Zechariah son of Berechiah (Barachiah in Greek), the post-exilic minor prophet named in Zechariah 1:1, about whom no death-by-murder tradition survives anywhere in scripture or elsewhere; and Zechariah son of Jehoiada, a priest stoned to death in the Temple court by order of King Joash for denouncing the nation's idolatry (2 Chronicles 24:20-22) — a death that matches Matthew's location and manner exactly, and that stood, in the traditional (though not universal) ordering of the Hebrew canon with Chronicles last, as the final murder recorded in the Hebrew Bible, mirroring Abel's position as the first. Since Chronicles' Zechariah is explicitly called "son of Jehoiada," not "son of Barachiah," most modern commentators read Matthew 23:35 as a conflation — either an error, a scribal harmonization with the better-known prophet's name, or (on one line of argument) deliberate, since Matthew is about to quote Zechariah 11:12-13 by name three chapters later, at 27:9-10 (see JEREMIAH). W.D. Davies and Dale C. Allison, Jr., A Critical and Exegetical Commentary on the Gospel According to Saint Matthew, vol. 3 (International Critical Commentary; Edinburgh: T&T Clark, 1997), surveys these competing identifications in its treatment of 23:35 (page not verified).

Cited in: Matthew 23:35.
